sample_q_texts: Gut microbiota-targeted probiotics are emerging as effective therapy for various metabolic disorders and their mechanisms are multifaceted and largely unexplored. Studies have shown that dysbiosis contributes to the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes, and other intestinal diseases, and that probiotics alleviate these conditions. However, current probiotic research uses enteric bacteria, which lack the ecological and functional complexity of a complex microbial community in the human gut. Here, we use live-cultured bacteria (in situ) to investigate (i) the effects of gut microbiota composition on the molecular outcomes of probiotic supplements; (ii) the mechanisms responsible for the microbiota effects; and (iii) the influence of probiotic supplement type on microbiota dynamics, including the transformation of stable colonizers and the recruitment of new taxa. Our data demonstrate that individual gut microbiota components alter the health outcomes in proportion to their microbial cross-talk, whereas probiotic supplement content does not change this mechanism. Therefore, it seems that the effect of a probiotic supplement is a consequence of the composition of the original fecal microbiota from which they are isolated. This is facilitated by its mucosal colonization and that its genus-level taxonomic distribution is typically similar in the first day of incubation. However, bacterial recruitment can occur at more extended time and higher incubation temperatures if, at the onset of the adaptation, the original colonizing microbes are not genetically represented in the host (inducible or non-targeted to the gut).

Free living large intestine microbes transform many dietary macromolecules into useful products including short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) at the descending colon. Due to the complexity of our natural diets and limited number of experimental and gene expression studies, we sought to identify novel components of the microbial community that are enriched in these short chain fatty acids. Metagenomic, single cell RNA sequencing and culture experiments were undertaken to determine the microbial community in the descending colon of the two common large cat species; domestic cat and domestic cow. Our first sequencing and culture studies revealed an unexpectedly broad microbial diversity of SCFA producing taxa within the gut of domestic animals. Additionally, we found differences in microbiome composition along the digestive tract of cats and cows, with most SCFA contributing bacteria found in the lower distal colon of both species. Our results indicated that the identified bacteria show functional similarities to those with physiological roles in early milk fermentation such as LacI, RseB and fucopinoindolamine 5-hydroxylase (FIAH), indicating SCFA producing bacteria could be useful in cultured dairy-derived SCFA precursors.

Microbial community colonization determines microbial ecology, and the dynamics of microbial community colonization are vital for ecology. Recent studies have extensively explored the processes, effects, and impacts of microbiome assembly dynamics. However, the scope of examining and quantifying microbial colonization in the human gut microbiota remains narrow. Our study focuses on the colonization of the human oral cavity microbiome in experimental human subjects, employing biochemical methods and Illumina's TruSight human oral microbiome panel. We assembled microbial community sequences, studied microbial community assembly dynamics, investigated systemic changes in microbial taxonomic and functional communities, and performed hierarchical agglomerative clustering on the complete microbiome. We assessed and quantified the genetic, abundance, and phylogenetic diversity of taxa in the oral cavity microbiome. Our results support three key findings: (1) a significant phenotypic plasticity in the oral microbiome composition; (2) a higher proportion of bacterial and fungal species with a functional profile of human commensal bacteria; and (3) a significantly lower proportion of the oral microbiome species diversity compared to the gut. Our statistical analysis of the multi-taxonomy analysis revealed that 1164 and 223 species were shared between gut and oral cavity metagenomes, whereas there were only 873 and 514 shared species between the gut and oral cavity. We then found that the fecal [corrected] oral cavity microbiome related to oral systemic features (race, age, and gender). We additionally detected common microbiota profiles between oral and gut microbiome using machine learning, which offers the potential to investigate associated systemic characteristics. Our work on oral cavity microbiome samples integrated into the WHO Human Microbiome Project, led by the Human Microbiome Project Working Group, is valuable for expanding the study of microbiome assembly and ecology in both the oral and human gut microbiomes.

Prediction of genotypic microbiome compositions in fecal samples is an important step in linking microbial communities to medical conditions. Machine learning techniques have been explored for this task, with few being able to capture both gut environment and gut bacterial structure. To this end, we present AlphaBayes, a model that produces stable and reliable prediction results for gut microbiome composition of adult volunteers while being optimized for genotype and diversity. By focusing on microbiome composition with reference datasets of clinical and healthy donors, and adjusting for microbiome diversity, AlphaBayes reaches high accuracy in predicting bacterial groups even in well-cultivated subjects. AlphaBayes will likely be an important framework for the interpretation of fecal metagenomics, enabling exploration of genetic and environmental drivers of gut microbiomes and their influence on human health.

Fermented foods have been studied over many decades as a means of probiotic intervention, yet little research has examined the role of the intestinal microbiome in modulating probiotic populations and the potential for this niche exploitation by the gut microbiota. To better understand the importance of the gut microbiome and its impact on host immunity, we proposed to treat the SIBO gut microbial community with a defined probiotic blend that was delivered via metabolically-active peptide-based probiotics to suppress gut inflammation and normal microbiota composition. Using a fed- and fasted-stimulated model of colitis in 1026 young (five years old) Wistar rats, and a raised dietary omega-6 polyunsaturated fat diet model to evaluate these effects, we found that administration of a probiotic blend diet, including synbiotic combination, significantly modulated the relative abundance of Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, but not Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria, despite the inclusion of members within these phyla, similar to the results obtained in a wild-type diet. Consistently, diet composition modulated the relative abundance of mucins and various lipids within the intestines. Elevated levels of metabolites that are associated with increased mucin abundance were detected both in the jejunum and colon in response to diet, providing further evidence that dietary changes might represent a pharmacologic mechanism of action for synbiotic blend administration, even at such an early age. Further, we found that a diet that was high in fatty acids was able to reduce the potential for probiotics to upregulate inflammatory markers, highlighting that the development of probiotic delivery systems can be used to target bacteria and molecules that support the integrity of the gut microbiome. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that probiotics that contain synbiotic blends could be effective in the treatment and prevention of inflammation and other diseases of the gastrointestinal tract.

The gut microbiome is becoming increasingly recognized as an essential component of host health. While microbial composition has been well studied, a link between changes in microbiota and host metabolic health has not been demonstrated. To address this gap, we initiated a microbiome study where we quantified the most common Akkermansia spp., a predominant Firmicute, over time and across metabolic compartments including host genes and metabolites. We demonstrated that the microbiome of Dha15-rTg mice changed dramatically in the hour following intragastric introduction of butyrate, a potentially beneficial metabolite of butyrate-producing Firmicutes.

The abundance of individual Firmicutes members differed according to the proportion of methane-producing bacteria in the population, with specific changes being observed for Rumae. Furthermore, abundance of Rumae and two other major Firmicutes, Eubacterium_2_and_Gram_neg_ATCC26575_and_20948, differed according to the metabolic state and host genetic background. These findings suggested that metabolite and/or organism specific composition of the gut microbiome is context-dependent, as predicted from microbial interactions within the microbiome.

These results are particularly pertinent given that gut microbial composition may act as an organ-specific reservoir of pathogenic potential.

IntroductionThe human colon is a complex ecosystem, where microbial communities interact with mucosal epithelial cells to produce a multi-faceted metabolite profile. With rapid advances in microbiome sequencing techniques, natural sample collections from human colon have become rapidly available. However, our understanding of the colonic microbiome and the microbiome-epi-epidemiology interactions remains to be fully elucidated. Metabolomic profiles can reveal microbiome shifts by revealing the metabolomic fingerprints of microbiome states, among which mixtures of Metabolomics-Based Metabolite Profiling (MBMP) provide best performances for identifying biomarker signatures against microbiome diversity changes. In this study, we explored the heterogeneity of abdominal microbiome types and the relationship between microbiota. To address this, we aim to discover signature metabolites in the colon that are potentially related to gut microbiota diversity shifts. We first performed a natural sample survey using whole stool and smaller sample sizes, which revealed community size distributions shifted significantly after one week of stay in vivo. We also evaluated whether a spectrum of gut microbiota diversity can be identified in stool samples of subjects of different sizes before and after staying in vivo. While stools collected from small sample sizes were more variable, stools collected from large sample sizes were enriched in taxonomy, gene expression, and metabolite concentrations associated with the diversity shifts. Using published human gut microbiota metagenomic data sets as a reference, we extracted enriched diversity signatures from 30 healthy subjects and 59 clinically diagnosed colon diseases. Our analyses showed that: (1) bowel and enteroenteric access through healthy stool samples, or bowel diagnosis impacted metabolite profiles. Therefore, all individual samples of this study revealed a relative enrichment in specific metabolites with low variance in analyses, (2) most microbiome diversity signatures enriched in the signature peptide taurine, taurine deficiency, butyrate, and inorganic nitrogen (atp), and matched those described previously, (3) underrepresented markers included glycerides and organic acids. These results suggest that bacterial enzyme activities can modulate the composition of metabolites in gut microbiome.

Monosaccharides (monosaccharides) are inherently unstable and susceptible to degradation by extracellular enzymes in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. However, carbohydrates interact with intestinal enterocytes (ColoEnTs) to prevent the development of dysbiosis. To better understand the role of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) on these interactions, we have assessed the relationship between metabolic-based microbiota dynamics and GAGs' degradation, exposure, and interaction in colon and bladder tissues. We characterized the composition, abundance, and metabolic activities of butyrate-producing colonic bacteria. Inhibition of fructose-6-phosphate epimerases in colonic fucopentaose (FP) biosynthesis reversed colonic fructose intake and induced colonic glycolysis, indicating the importance of fructose metabolism in colonic gut health. In response to gut emptying, colonic F-6-P epimerases encoded by Bacillus bifidobacterium and Escherichia coli switch to a stronger preference for product conversion, despite the presence of both microbes. We found that increases in butyrate production decreased F6-P epimerase activity, supporting a trade-off between metabolic flexibility and maintenance of short-chain fatty acids. Following dehydration, colonic F-6-P epimerases increased their activity, suggesting that F-6-P degradation through exoglycosidases is a means to detoxify glucose. Our studies highlight the role of colonic GAGs and their interaction with colonic bacteria in exacerbating F-6-P epimerase activity and intestinal metabolism.

The human skin microbiome is implicated in health and disease, but its main biological features, including structure, interspecies variation, and stability are poorly studied. We sequenced skin surface samples from a small segment of the human population in Spain and characterized the four major groups of the microbiome: microbial, fungal, psycho-biotic and physicochemical. Sex was not a significant driver of microbiome diversity. Our results suggest that this diversity is acquired through a complex suite of mechanisms, including transfer from donors to hosts. Low maturity affects the healthy newborn gut microbiome. Transferred bacterial species were associated with higher human health parameters, such as leukocyte functioning and survival and reduced chronic inflammation. We found that proteins of microbial origin played a role in one of the main antibiotic resistance mechanisms of bacterial growth.

BackgroundThe majority of the microbiome remains unknown in the human gut. Understanding how microbiomes shape host physiology has relevance for the management of chronic inflammatory diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Utilizing high-density 16S rRNA sequencing and biased filtering to identify viral-associated microbial taxa, we sought to differentiate the contributions of viral-associated and truly bacterial phyla of colonic bacteria from an IBD cohort.

MethodTo perform our analysis, we sequenced the mid-gut (DQ-32) and caecum (DQ-31) microbiomes of 40 IBD subjects and their healthy controls. Additionally, three other IBD subjects were sequenced for companion studies. Metagenome coverage was 16S rRNA, and a version of the 16S rRNA gene-specific marker DE35 with taxa and origins more frequently sampled in the GC/regions. Mutation analyses identified expected short-term impacts by objectively identifying and quantifying differences in four specific taxa of de novo sequences. A Spearman correlation matrix was generated to identify associations between taxa and antibody, chemokine, and cytokine production.

ResultsBoth DQ-32 and DQ-31 microbiomes were diverse and host-specific in terms of composition and alpha diversity. The study showed no significant differences in abundance between host bacteria in DQ-32 and DQ-31, although the TaqMan-based analysis of viral transcripts revealed that the two haplotypes associated with IBD included more bacteriophages than true-host bacterial sequences. We found no significant correlation between host or pathogen abundance and antibody, chemokine, or cytokine expression.

SummaryThe human microbiome composition of DQ-32 and DQ-31 differs significantly from DQ-31. However, we have not yet detected any association between CD8+ lymphocyte phenotype or COVID-19 antibody responses and viral-associated bacterial sequences. We confirmed earlier findings of hyperdiversity among bacterivorous viral sequences. Given the large proportion of phages, prophages, and endogenous host components of DQ-32 and DQ-31, we conclude that further analyses of colonic communities are needed to further resolve the composition of the mammalian gut microbiome.

Mediation analysis has emerged as a versatile tool for answering mechanistic questions in microbiome research because it provides a statistical framework for attributing treatment effects to alternative causal pathways. Using a series of linked regressions, this analysis quantifies how complementary data relate to one another and respond to treatments. Despite these advances, existing softwares rigid assumptions often result in users viewing mediation analysis as a black box. We designed the multimedia R package to make advanced mediation analysis techniques accessible, ensuring that statistical components are interpretable and adaptable. The package provides a uniform interface to direct and indirect effect estimation, synthetic null hypothesis testing, bootstrap confidence interval construction, and sensitivity analysis, enabling experimentation with various mediator and outcome models while maintaining a simple overall workflow. The software includes modules for regularized linear, compositional, random forest, hierarchical, and hurdle modeling, making it well-suited to microbiome data. We illustrate the package through two case studies. The first re-analyzes a study of the microbiome and metabolome of Inflammatory Bowel Disease patients, uncovering potential mechanistic interactions between the microbiome and disease-associated metabolites, not found in the original study. The second analyzes new data about the influence of mindfulness practice on the microbiome. The mediation analysis highlights shifts in taxa previously associated with depression that cannot be explained indirectly by diet or sleep behaviors alone. A gallery of examples and further documentation can be found at https://go.wisc.edu/830110.

IMPORTANCEMicrobiome studies routinely gather complementary data to capture different aspects of a microbiomes response to a change, such as the introduction of a therapeutic. Mediation analysis clarifies the extent to which responses occur sequentially via mediators, thereby supporting causal, rather than purely descriptive, interpretation. multimedia is a modular R package with close ties to the wider microbiome software ecosystem that makes statistically rigorous, flexible mediation analysis easily accessible, setting the stage for precise and causally informed microbiome engineering.

The microbiome represents a complex community of trillions of microorganisms residing in various body parts, and plays critical roles in maintaining host health and well-being. Understanding the interactions between microbiota and host offers valuable insights into potential strategies to promote health, including microbiome-targeted interventions. We have created MicrobiomeKG, a Knowledge Graph for microbiome research, bridging various taxa and microbial pathways with host health. This novel knowledge graph derives algorithmically-generated knowledge assertions from the supplemental tables supporting published microbiome papers, and is deployed for integrative analysis and hypothesis generation via the Biomedical Data Translator ecosystem.

Bacterial vaginosis (BV) affects approximately 29% of women in the U.S., with higher rates among certain demographics and up to 50% recurrence within a year. Besides complications like increased risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), pregnancy-related issues, it can negatively impact psychological well-being, leading to discomfort and reduced quality of life. While previous studies have provided insights into the overall metabolomic profile of healthy and diseased vaginal environments, the elucidation of individual microbial metabolite signatures remains limited. Furthermore, given that biofilms exhibit distinct metabolic requirements compared to planktonic cultures, a differential analysis of metabolites in both growth conditions could reveal potential therapeutic targets. This study presents a comprehensive metabolomic analysis and comparison of significant vaginal microbes including Lactobacillus crispatus, Gardenerella vaginalis, and Lactobacillus iners in both planktonic and biofilm growth conditions. Our analysis revealed distinct metabolite production and consumption patterns among different microbes and growth modes. In biofilm cultures, metabolite consumption is influenced by nutrient availability, which in turn regulates the profile of produced metabolites. G. vaginalis demonstrated the ability to form biofilms in various media types. Limited shared metabolic pathways in both biofilm types of G. vaginalis, highlights the unique metabolic processes involved in their formation. Despite L. crispatus suspension and biofilm cultures sharing 142 consumed and 104 produced metabolites, the biofilm culture demonstrated a remarkable metabolic shift. While comparing suspension and biofilm cultures of L. crispatus, L. iners, and G. vaginalis, we found convergence in nutrient utilization, but divergence in metabolic outputs reflecting growth-specific adaptations and underscore the importance of considering the state of existence when studying the vaginal microbiome.

This study provides valuable insights into the growth mode-specific metabolic requirements of key vaginal microbes. The findings underscore the potential for leveraging metabolite-mediated microbial cross-talk as a novel therapeutic approach against BV. This avenue of research warrants further investigation, as it could lead to the development of targeted interventions that modulate the vaginal microbiome through metabolic manipulation, potentially offering more effective and personalized treatments for BV.

Studies investigating microbial temporal dynamics are increasingly common, leveraging longitudinal designs that collect microbial abundance data across multiple time points from the same subjects. Traditional exploratory approaches like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) fail to fully utilize this structure. By organizing data as a three-way array--subjects as rows, microbial abundances as columns, and time points as the third dimension--multi-way methods such as Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) can better capture temporal and structural patterns. This study demonstrates Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) as a method to explore longitudinal microbiome data using three exemplary studies.

In the first example, a long time series of in vitro microbiomes, PARAFAC identifies primary time-resolved variations. The second example, a longitudinal infant gut microbiome study, shows that PARAFAC can distinguish subject groups and enhance comparative analysis, even with moderate missing data. In the third example, a gingivitis intervention study of the oral microbiome, PARAFAC enables the identification of microbial subcommunities of interest through post-hoc clustering.

These examples highlight PARAFACs broad applicability for analysing longitudinal microbiome data across diverse environments. The approach is implemented in the R package parafac4microbiome, available on CRAN, providing researchers with accessible tools for similar analyses.

ImportanceUnderstanding how microbiomes change over time can give us valuable insights into their role in health and disease. Many traditional methods like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) miss important patterns in data collected over time, but Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) helps uncover these trends in a much clearer way. Using this approach, we were able to identify key changes in microbiomes across different settings, like lab experiments, the infant gut, and the mouth. PARAFAC also works well even when some data is missing, which is a common issue. To make this tool accessible, we have included it in a user-friendly R package, enabling other researchers to analyse microbiome dynamics in their own studies and explore how these changes might influence health and treatments.

Microbial communities significantly impact medicine, biotechnology, and agriculture. Advanced sequencing technologies have generated extensive microbiome data, enabling the discovery of substantial evolutionary and ecological patterns. However, traditional supervised learning methods struggle to capture universal patterns in microbial community data, largely due to the large data heterogeneity and profound batch effects among samples, rendering it difficult to classify samples as well as detect biomarkers from millions of samples, not to say the intricate but important dynamic patterns from a variety of contextualized sceneries. In this study, we propose MGM, a context-aware, attention-based foundation model, pre-trained on a dataset of 263,302 microbiome samples (Microcorpus-260K) via language modeling. MGM demonstrated significant improvements in microbial community classification compared to traditional machine learning methods. Additionally, MGM has enabled contextualized classification, effectively overcomes cross-regional limitations, showing enhanced performance on intercontinental datasets through transfer learning. Furthermore, fine-tuning MGM on a longitudinal infant dataset revealed distinct keystone genera during development, with Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium exhibiting higher attention weights in vaginal deliveries, and Haemophilus in cesarean deliveries. Finally, through in silico modeling, the model also uncovered novel microbial dynamic patterns in a Crohn disease cohort following antibiotic treatment. In conclusion, by leveraging self-attention and autoregressive pre-training, MGM serves as a versatile model for various downstream microbiome tasks and holds significant potential for achieving contextualized aims.

Recent studies have observed an association between genital tract microbiota and reproductive outcomes in patients undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF). This finding could be caused by ascending dysbiosis from the vagina to the endometrium. The main objective of this study was to compare the microbiota and total bacterial load in the vagina, cervix and endometrium of IVF patients and oocyte donors. Thus, a total of two cohorts were explored: IVF patients (N=27) and healthy oocyte donors (N=26). The microbiota was investigated using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of the V3-V4 hypervariable regions, as well as qPCR for common vaginal species and total bacterial load. The study used a transcervical sampling approach for the endometrial microbiota samples.

The highest bacterial load was seen in the vagina (median 2.6*109; 95% CI 9.7*108 - 7.1*109; 16S rRNA gene copies/swab), followed by the cervix (median 9.0*107; 95% CI 3.3*107 - 2.4*108; 16S rRNA gene copies/swab) and the endometrium (median 8.6*106; 95%CI 3.1*106 - 2.4*107; 16S rRNA gene copies/swab). Only 1% of the observed variation between genital tract samples was explained by patient group (IVF patient or oocyte donor) and less than 1% of the variation between genital tract samples was explained by the anatomical site. Although, findings could be impacted by the transcervical sampling approach, 16S rRNA gene sequencing as well as species-specific qPCR showed a similar microbiota composition present in the cervix and the endometrium when compared to the vaginal microbiota.

MotivationUnderstanding the associations between traits and microbial composition is a fundamental objective in microbiome research. Recently, researchers have turned to machine learning (ML) models to achieve this goal with promising results. However, the effectiveness of advanced ML models is often limited by the unique characteristics of microbiome data, which are typically high-dimensional, compositional, and imbalanced. These characteristics can hinder the models ability to fully explore the relationships among taxa in predictive analyses. To address this challenge, data augmentation has become crucial. It involves generating synthetic samples with artificial labels based on existing data and incorporating these samples into the training set to improve ML model performance.

ResultsHere we propose PhyloMix, a novel data augmentation method specifically designed for microbiome data to enhance predictive analyses. PhyloMix leverages the phylogenetic relationships among microbiome taxa as an informative prior to guide the generation of synthetic microbial samples. Leveraging phylogeny, PhyloMix creates new samples by removing a subtree from one sample and combining it with the corresponding subtree from another sample. Notably, PhyloMix is designed to address the compositional nature of microbiome data, effectively handling both raw counts and relative abundances. This approach introduces sufficient diversity into the augmented samples, leading to improved predictive performance. We empirically evaluated PhyloMix on six real microbiome datasets across five commonly used ML models. PhyloMix significantly outperforms distinct baseline methods including sample-mixing-based data augmentation techniques like vanilla mixup and compositional cutmix, as well as the phylogeny-based method TADA. We also demonstrated the wide applicability of PhyloMix in both supervised learning and contrastive representation learning.

AvailabilityThe Apache licensed source code is available at (https://github.com/batmen-lab/phylomix).

Large sex hormonal fluctuations are thought to influence vaginal microbiota, but little is known about the impact of small, physiological variations. Here we tracked changes in vaginal microbiota during four key menstrual cycle phases in 61 healthy Italian women from the Women4Health cohort. The microbiota was primarily composed of Lactobacillus, with L. iners being the most abundant. Noteworthy, the high abundance of L. iners contrasts with previous studies in European populations, challenging its proposed pathogenic role, and suggesting distinct microbiota profiles within Europe. Individual microbiotas were generally stable, but beta diversity was higher during the follicular phase. Only 11 women exhibited compositional shifts and those mostly occurred between follicular and ovulatory phases. Finally, among the hormones evaluated, 17-beta estradiol had the largest impact on taxa abundance variations. Our study highlights specific features of the Italian population and points to the resilience of the vaginal microbiota to physiological hormonal changes.

The urinary microbiome, or urobiome, is a novel area of research that has been gaining attention recently, as urine was thought to be sterile for years. There is limited information about the composition of the urobiome in health and disease. The urobiome may be affected by several factors and diseases such as diabetes, a disease that often leads to kidney damage. Thus, we need to understand the role of the urobiome to assess and monitor kidney disease related to diabetes over time. We conducted a systematic review to summarize knowledge about the urobiome in association with diabetes mellitus and diabetic kidney disease. The search, conducted in PubMed and Web of Science electronic databases until July 2024, resulted in the selection of 18 studies including cross-sectional case-control studies, cross-sectional surveys and one prospective longitudinal study. In total, the urobiome of 1,571 people was sequenced, of which 662 people had diabetes, and of these 36 had confirmed diabetic kidney disease; 609 were healthy individuals, 179 had prediabetes or were at risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus and 121 did not have diabetes but had other comorbidities. Eight studies analysed data from females, one was focused on male data, and the other nine had mixed female-male data. Most of the studies had a small sample size, used voided midstream urine, and used 16S rRNA sequencing. This systematic review summarizes trends seen throughout published data available to have a first baseline knowledge of the urinary microbiome, and its microbiota, in association with diabetes.

Ruminant products are consumed widely on a global level due to their high protein and micronutrient density. However, ruminant production is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly with respect to methane (CH), with ruminants contributing 33% of all anthropogenic CH emissions. CH is produced due to the natural fermentative processes undertaken by the complex rumen microbiome, primarily via the utilisation of hydrogen by rumen archaea to form CH. Previous studies have shown that feeding the red seaweed Asparagopsis taxiformis (ASP) to ruminants can reduce CHemissions from beef cattle by up to 80% (Roque et al., 2021). Nevertheless, the mechanism of action of this seaweed in terms of effects on the rumen microbiome is largely unknown, which is the main focus of this study. Six Nordic Red cows at 122 {+/-} 13.7 (mean {+/-} SD) days in milk were divided into 3 blocks by milk yield in Latin square design and fed grass silage and a commercial concentrate (60:40) either with or without 0.5% ASP on an organic matter basis. Rumen fluid was collected 19 days into each experimental period, with a holistic approach using both assembly and read mapping based approaches to interrogate taxonomic, functional, and ecological shifts applied to metagenomic data. We show that ASP reduces methane production not only through direct inhibition of methanogens but also by disrupting cobamide-dependent metabolic pathways and redirecting carbon flow toward pyruvate and propionate rather than acetate and methane. For the first time, specific enzymes involved in vitamin B12 (cobamide) biosynthesis are identified as suppressed by ASP, and microbial taxa contributing to these functional changes are elucidated showing both niche displacement and resilience within the rumen microbiome. These findings offer new mechanistic insight into how red seaweed supplementation modulates the rumen microbiome, supporting its potential role in sustainable ruminant production.

sample_q_texts: Activity patterns emerge and are driven by environmental signals through the synaptic transmission process of changes in the firing rate, current magnitude, and frequency of oscillations during deep sleep. However, neuronal activity during continuous wakefulness and slow-wave sleep varies significantly and is not substantially dependent on one another. Here, using purified forms of Ambigram neurons from hippocampal and prefrontal cortex, we measure the impact of external noise on GABA-mediated neural activity in awake behaving mice. Consistent with previous observations, noise increased current output and amplitude but decreased stable component rate across both brain regions. Interestingly, this effects were strongest and most pronounced in the am-glutamate neuron layer. We suggest that changes in firing rates, low-frequency synaptic activity, and receptive field amplitude, should be understood within the context of different neural population compositions during sleep.

Understanding the outcome of environments-dependent plasticity should be in addition to considering neural mechanisms, as this shapes brain development across all types of organisms. Indeed, many open questions in the field concern the neural underpinnings of individual differences in environmental plasticity. Here, we present a novel method for studying this mechanism: computational integration of brain-wide activity and visual response data from functional brain imaging. This technique, utilizing multi-level network in- and out-depolarizations, allows for an integrative integration of both state of brain activity and functional connectivity. We apply this approach to a single animal: the zebrafish, a vertebrate model with a flexible visual system for assessing plasticity to perturbations in the visual field. We use a model of "early visual cortex plasticity", whereby zebrafish respond to visual cues over a short and a long latency. Our results demonstrate strong plasticity over the latency, and rapid shifts in stable dynamics. The plasticity of the zebrafish visual system enables behavioral responses to stimulus-changing visual fields. Our integrative approach allows us to gain novel insights into the role of plasticity for cognition and behavior, and how the structure of these behaviors depend on the brain.

Shifting the sensitivity of a system to variations in input variables to either reduce its effect on the system output, or prevent it from manifesting, typically to the detriment of its performance. This type of sensitivity adaption has been shown to function effectively as a learning paradigm in systems, where we can harness the efficient activation dynamics of spike-timing-dependent plasticity to train systems to respond to stimuli that are intrinsically rewarding, only responding to inputs over relatively small windows of time, or reactivate a system after a temporary block, etc.

Our research brings together neurobiological, imaging, machine learning, and behavioral techniques to uncover the learning, reinforcement, and reward mechanisms that underpin pattern-based learning - a challenging task which meets increasing demand as neuromorphic systems seek to achieve human-like behaviour. We built a dataset that catalogues behaviorally-relevant neural activity in an animal model using electrophysiology, position-tracking, and visual reinforcement.

We adapted a reinforcement learning toolbox to simultaneously determine activity levels, behavior on the output trials, and the amount of reward earned from each trial. This allowed us to quantitatively test a number of hypotheses, including how the feedforward and synaptic plasticity networks effect the learning and activation dynamics of hippocampal spike-timing-dependent plasticity. We also observed robust changes in activity-dependent variables as a result of conditioning.

These findings reveal how pattern-based learning is conceptualised at the level of activity dynamics, using an integrated data-driven-machine learning pipeline and applying a reward-driven adaptation paradigm that enhances the activation learning mechanism.

Intra- and inter-temporal choice can be used to study different types of selfish behaviors, and both selfish and altruistic decision-makers are aware of their environment and the costs they may face for their decision-making. In animals, ranging from fruit flies to monkeys, behaviors as complex and cognitively difficult as tradeoffs can be explored. In particular, many research labs have been exploring exactly how this framework can be applied to the ability to formulate and pursue trade-offs, using a series of studies on wayward and desynchronized neurons to test the reliability of such decision-making. In particular, we have found that locally biased neurons fire earlier, when players can effectively ignore potential costs, in a so-called 'desynchronized' context compared to players with full neuromodulatory coverage. Using these studies, we seek to characterize this setup as a 'desynchronized context' for multiregulatory (collective) decision-making. In this manuscript we discuss the plasticity of desynchronization as observed across sensory systems and highlight how disentangling this plasticity can better explain how patterns of stimulation, across models, can affect the perception of desynchronization.

Neuronal activity generates large-scale patterns that drive cognition, conscious experience, and behaviors. However, the brain suppresses reliable and precise neural signals to enable top-down control over most of these patterns. Precise brain activity restoration techniques offer strategies to optimize the encoding and decoding of neural signals across multiple stages of execution, thereby allowing similar encoding mechanisms to the suppressed signals for centralized action execution. Spontaneous bursting (SBB) provides one such technique, in which neurons burst at high frequency to encode and decode massive networks over wide intervals, allowing us to explore a high-resolution neural process and gain insights into the function of the brain. Specifically, we asked whether spontaneous bursting can mediate power-law adaptation, a central property of neural reward processing, under moderate levels of reward. The power law is the first universal behavioral adaptation scale, which predicts that the amount of adaptation through behavior is inversely proportional to the reward value, similar to the specific neuronal system underlying SBB. We hypothesized that stimulation at a fast rate (SBB) would ensure the precise distribution of stimulation applied across stimulation events and therefore promote power law adaptation. To test this hypothesis, we used optogenetic and electrophysiological tools to stimulate the visual cortex under moderate reward levels (reward value = 40%) across spatially separated neurons and to examine the role of SBB in enhancing power-law adaptation. We recorded neurobehavioral responses under different reward levels, demonstrating that visual cortex neurons self-activate and adapt under both slow and fast SBB stimulation levels. Additionally, we could observe the effects of repeating SBB stimulation patterns on power law adaptation, suggesting that SBB may mediate the structure of adaptation. Together, our results demonstrate the potential of SBB as a valuable tool for understanding the function of neuronal circuitry by exposing the timing and timing of brain activity to selective strengthening stimuli in the cortex in real-time.

Nootropics enhance learning and working memory by reducing subjective brain activity and increasing neural connectivity. A general consensus holds that neural noise, or background activity, exerts powerful influences on brain function. Yet, the mechanisms underlying this neuroplasticity remain poorly understood. In particular, little is known about how neural inhibition impacts underlying neural activity. To address this, we isolated neurons in the mossy fiber pathway in the primary visual cortex (V1) and discovered that rapid gamma motor neurons inhibit key lateral cortical and subcortical inhibitory neurons. Through a combination of optogenetics and network-based computational models, we identified the direct downstream target region for gamma motor neurons, a pyramidal cell, as a key putative candidate. Our current model recapitulates the observed differences between excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and illustrates an altered calcium regulatory system in gamma motor neurons, which may underlie how V1 inhibition inhibits visual function. Our data provide fundamental new insights into the underlying mechanisms that act to selectively modulate neural activity.

Animal behaviors are governed by a global set of neural circuits comprising several tens of thousands of interneurons. Converging evidence suggests that these circuits produce dynamical rhythms in synchronous firing activity. This state is associated with the well-established efficient display of normal behavior. Here we used two-photon calcium imaging to record synchronized dynamics of mouse pedunculopontine tegmental (PPT) neurons in vivo at three timescales: 1) local timescale, 2) local and midbrain timescale, and 3) global timescale. We found a robust common rhythm in synchronized low frequency oscillations, and a >30-fold range in periodicity. The region within the precuneus displaying most synchronous firing displayed a very short interneuronal distance and strong synchrony. These dynamical rhythms were associated with a mouse behavioral task, akin to domain adaptation to navigate and find an exit. Extensive co-localization of sensory, sensorimotor, and reward circuits alongside of synchronized firing shows a relationship between interneuronal firing dynamics, behavioral pattern, and context.

It has been hypothesized that the spatiotemporal aggregation of cells, proteins, and molecules across the brain depends on  schedules of activation and inhibition induced by the ascending and descending nervous systems.  A common feature of these dynamics is called oscillatory synchrony between successive neurons. In conscious states such as wakefulness, these oscillations are most commonly observed between oscillatory and inhibitory neuron assemblies. Here, we show that in regions of the cerebellum, coordinated oscillations between cells within GABAergic systems represent a sensory-driven means to detect and respond to fear and reward-related stimuli. Further, these oscillations depend on the occurrence of competing inhibitory and excitatory neuronal ensembles; collectively, they comprise "paired-oscillatory rhythms" that are also observed during sleep. This hypothesis is also supported by experiments showing that experimentally-induced modulations of neuronal inhibition (in this study, inhibition by 7 and 10 minute thalamus-nuclei inactivating GABAergic neurons) result in efferent (i.e., a-kind) oscillations between inhibitory and glutamatergic neuronal assemblies in the cerebellum. In addition, we find that the observed co-circulating integrated excitation and inhibition represent a specific configuration of network activity and content, supporting our hypothesis that associative information is acquired and encoded by oscillatory synchrony between successive neurons. Together, the observed oscillations help generate an integrated conceptual map in the cerebellum, and support aversive processing according to predictions made by behavior model theories of conscious perception and decision-making.

Significance statementTo perceive an external stimulus or a mentally imagined event, neural representations require the sum of synaptic inhibition and excitation at a successful pattern. Experiments have shown that a steady state of inhibitions and excitation oscillations can sustain this type of representation. We show in experimental animals how the neuronal interactions occurring during these oscillations sustain these types of representations. Our computational models predict that a transient oscillation of an excitatory neuronal cell will promote its own in a manner analogous to a short hop reflex that the cerebellum models in the rat. The need to aggregate inhibitory and excitatory neuronal assemblies explains the synchrony observed in the learning and behavior models and provides a new mechanistic explanation for interlinked circuit dynamics, especially the network-level, combinatorial, and non-neuronal contributions that constitute their input/output relationships.

In the brain, synaptic activity is necessary for learning. Despite the importance of short-term synaptic plasticity (SSTP) in learning, little is known about its underlying mechanisms. In particular, the physical changes responsible for such activity are poorly understood. Here, using single-neuron electrophysiology from a recently developed ensemble method that allowed to single-unit recording in a head-fixed rat brain, we analysed activity in different neuronal cell groups during learning of a classical Pavlovian task. As measured by statistical physics, we found that individual neurons were responsive to changes in the stimulus rate during learning but were rather insensitiveto changes in the feedback signaling. Furthermore, all neurons were more plastic over the learning course than the rest of the population. That plasticity was not influenced by electrical and chemical recovery as the boost in plasticity remained detectable despite inactivation of a drug with selective inhibition of NMDA receptor. This led us to investigate the central targets of the downregulation and depolarizations that preceded synaptic rearrangements. We report that the inhibition decreased neuronal target activation as well as the degree of changes in activity. In contrast, increases in activity were associated with the upregulation of neuroregulatory factors that can stimulate plasticity.

Plasticity is a key property of neural circuits but current biophysical descriptions are incomplete. We develop a tractable two-dimensional (2D) model of tuning-dependent adaptation of synaptic weights and iontophase firing rates to stress.

This model incorporates drift and voltage-sensitive stimulation (SSS) that responds to chemical cues at physiological thresholds, attenuates drift within cells by complex iontophase processes and reconfigures synaptic weights on long timescale. We describe a simple numerical experiment that demonstrates these properties within a single network model. The models plasticity can be tuned to match sensory experience to vision for filtering in rod-cone or color-cone networks, to enhanced number of responding cells in motor pathways or fear-evoking pathways, and to protection against epilepsy.

These simple systems illustrate properties of neural function that are elusive for biophysical understanding at any level. We demonstrate how these subtle connections give rise to stereotyped functional organization, plasticity, and functioning across complex neural systems.
sample_p_texts: The ability to detect unanticipated, novel events and rapidly relay this information across neural networks is fundamental to brain function, enabling the selection of appropriate behavioral responses. Here, we examine the transmission of holographically triggered action potentials in primary visual cortex of quietly resting mice, focusing on the dynamics of communication from pyramidal neurons. We demonstrate that these novel action potentials, which are uncorrelated with preceding activity, exert a disproportionally large influence on neighboring neurons. Their influence scales robustly to an exponent between 0.2 and 0.3 relative to their number. Remarkably, even a small number of novel action potentials can engage a majority of the local network, achieving high decoding accuracy of the perturbation origin in the face of high trial-by-trial variability and ongoing activity characterized by scale-invariant, parabolic neuronal avalanches. This heightened susceptibility to small, local perturbations aligns with the behavior of complex systems exhibiting critical dynamics. Our findings reveal that scaling underpins the efficient communication of unanticipated action potentials, suggesting it is a fundamental mechanism for detecting and processing novel events in the brain. These results provide new insights into the neural basis of novelty detection and highlight the importance of critical dynamics in cortical network function.

Much of our understanding of how neural circuit activity relates to human behaviour as well as mental health stems from non-invasive assessments of the central nervous system. Further progress in key questions, however, requires a higher differentiation of circuit-level activity, which remains constrained by the sensitivity and resolution of existing instruments. Here we show that neural quantum sensing with optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) addresses this issue by significantly outperforming EEG and conventional MEG in both signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and signal coherence across trials. SNR for OPMs was increased by up to 205% compared to EEG and by up to 40% compared to conventional MEG. Likewise, the signal coherence across trials of OPMs was increased by up to 61% compared to EEG and by up to 23% compared to conventional MEG. Our data emphasize the important role of OPMs for non-invasive neuroimaging, paving the way for significant advances in basic research as well as translational applications.

During wake, sound-evoked and spontaneous neural activity of the auditory cortex evolve in distinct subspaces whereas anesthesia disrupts sound responses and merges these spaces. To evaluate if similar modifications of the sound representation geometry explain sensory disconnection during sleep, we followed large neural populations of the mouse auditory cortex across slow wave sleep and wakefulness. We observed that sleep dampens sound responses but preserves the geometry of sound representations which remain separate from spontaneous activity. Moreover, response dampening was strongly coordinated across neurons and varied throughout sleep spanning from fully preserved response patterns to population response failures on a fraction of sound presentations. These failures are more common during high spindle-band activity and more rarely observed in wakefulness. Therefore, in sleep, the auditory system preserves sound feature selectivity up to the cortex for detailed acoustic surveillance, but concurrently implements an intermittent gating mechanism leading to local sensory disconnections.

Adaptation is a common neural phenomenon wherein sustained stimulation evokes fewer action potentials (spikes) over time. Rather than simply reduce firing rate, adaptation may help neurons form better (i.e. more discriminable) representations of sensory input. To study effects of adaptation in low-threshold mechanoreceptors (LTMRs), we recorded single unit LTMR responses to 30-second-long vibrotactile stimuli with different intensities and frequencies applied to the hind paw of rats. To assess the impact of adaptation on somatosensory encoding, decoders were applied to the initial and late (adapted) phases of population-level responses to assess the decodability (discrimination) of stimulus intensity and frequency. Adaptation-mediated changes in the rate and timing (phase-locking) of spikes were quantified. Rate coding of stimulus intensity was improved by the nonuniform reduction in firing rate across responses to different stimuli, and across neurons. This improvement was absent in simulations with uniform reductions in firing rate, thus revealing the necessity of stimulus-dependent variability in adaptation effects. Spike timing (quantified as interspike intervals) remained highly informative about stimulus frequency throughout stimulation despite the progressive reduction in spike count over time. When the drop in spike count was accounted for, adaptation was found to improve temporal coding of stimulus frequency by increasing the precision of phase-locking. In other words, adaptation improved the precision of spike timing, and this increased the information about stimulus frequency conveyed by each spike. These results show that adaptation, by modulating spiking in different ways, can improve encoding of different stimulus features using different coding schemes.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENTFiring rate adaptation refers to the progressive reduction in spiking during sustained stimulation. Adaptation is often ascribed to fatigue and could conceivably introduce ambiguity into neural representations by causing (the probability or timing of) spike generation to depend not only on the current stimulus, but also on past stimulation. By recording from rat primary somatosensory afferents during vibrotactile stimulation of the paw, we show that nonuniform adaptation across sets of afferents improves rate-based coding of stimulus intensity. We also show that adaptation improves spike timing (phase-locking to a periodic stimulus) which, in turn, improves temporal coding of stimulus frequency. These results demonstrate that early-stage adaptation improves somatosensory signals relayed centrally.

Sensory input and internal context converge onto the hippocampus as spatio-temporal activity patterns. Transitions in these input patterns are frequently salient. We demonstrate that short-term potentiation (STP) mediates escape from EI balance to implement mismatch detection in spatiotemporally patterned activity sequences. We characterized STP in the mouse hippocampus CA3-CA1 network using optogenetic patterned stimuli in CA3 while recording from CA1 pyramidal neurons. STP modulates EI summation across patterns, first amplifying, then reducing responses. We parameterized a multiscale model of network projections onto hundreds of E and I boutons on a CA1 neuron, each including stochastic signaling to mediate STP. The model detected mismatches in trains of input patterns, which we experimentally confirmed. Mismatch selectivity depends on pattern sparsity, network weights, and connectivity, and neuronal spiking makes it sharper. Finally, we predict strong mismatch detection for gamma-frequency bursts between theta cycles, consistent with theta-tuned snapshots of novel input.

Synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus is fundamental to learning and memory, yet few studies examine how pattern learning occurs across multiple synapses. Such cross-synapse learning is fundamental to emergent properties of pattern discrimination and generalisation, which depend on assumptions about independence of plasticity and linearity of summation. We used sparse optogenetic spatio-temporal  pattern stimulation in the CA3 coupled with postsynaptic depolarization to elicit plasticity on CA1 pyramidal neurons, and found that  trained patterns were selectively strengthened, but only in a subset of postsynaptic cells. Increased resting membrane potential and background mini-EPSP rates were predictive of learner cells. Summation following plasticity became more linear in learners compared to non-learners, consistent with the observed elevated post-stimulus hyperpolarization on non-learner cells. Thus our exploration of biologically plausible sparse activity supports pattern-selective learning, but in a heterogeneous manner modulated by both cell-intrinsic and network features.

The BraiDyn-BC (Brain Dynamics underlying emergence of Behavioral Change) Database offers an extensive, multimodal dataset that links wide-field calcium imaging of the mouse neocortex to comprehensive behavioral measurements during a behavioral task. As one of the contents in this database, we newly provide a dataset that includes 15 sessions spanning two weeks of motor skill learning, in which 25 mice were trained to pull a lever to obtain water rewards. Simultaneous high-speed videography captures body, facial, and eye movements, and environmental parameters are monitored. The dataset also features resting-state cortical activity and sensory-evoked responses, enhancing its utility for both learning-related and sensory-driven neural dynamics studies. Data are formatted in accordance with the Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) standard, ensuring compatibility with existing analysis tools and adherence to the FAIR principles. This resource enables in-depth investigations into the neural mechanisms underlying behavior and learning. The platform encourages collaborative research, supporting the exploration of rapid within-session learning effects, long-term behavioral adaptations, and neural circuit dynamics.

Hippocampal theta oscillations regulate the timing of neurons to support navigation, memory formation, and sensorimotor integration. Theta is modulated by running speed, breathing, whisking, and jumping and increases in tasks involving memory encoding or retrieval. The positive relationship between theta frequency and running speed is believed stabilize hippocampal representations of space amid movement variability. Here, we incorporated a novel string-pulling task to determine if established relationships between movement and theta hold when progress to a reward is determined by the length of string pulled. This task eliminates many speed-associated inputs, such vestibular, visual, and hindlimb information, and allows an unprecedented level of precision in the analysis of individual paw movements. Given that animals move the string a fixed length to acquire a reward, we predicted that the positive relationship between theta frequency and speed would hold.

ApproachFive Sprague Dawley rats (4 mo.) were trained to continuously pull a string a fixed distance of 208 cm using an automated string-pulling system and run on a track for food reward. Local-field data was acquired from electrodes in dorsal CA1.

ResultsRelationships between theta and movement speed were distinct during string pulling and running. While theta was robust in both conditions, frequency was significantly reduced during string-pulling and showed no speed-frequency coupling, unlike running. This difference could result from the conflict between hindlimb and forelimb signals, with only forelimb movement signaling advancement. Fine-grained analysis of paw movements during string-pulling (lift, advance, grasp, pull, push) revealed that theta power and frequency peaked during the contralateral paws downward push despite paw speed being low during this action. This suggests that theta frequency and power could respond to effort rather than purely kinematic information. Notably, running-associated theta may similarly reflect both speed and effort as most locomotor tasks conflate these variables. Finally, theta phase aligned from one reach-pull cycle to the next during the downward pull motion - the first action that directly advances the string forward. Since phase-locking has been associated with sensorimotor gating, synchrony at this point could reflect the gating of inputs that are the most causally relevant for reaching the reward, potentially facilitating integration of action-outcome signals for memory encoding and navigation. Taken together, these data support a dual-scale view of hippocampal processing and theta-band activity where macroscale theta activity requires suprathreshold sensory, vestibular, and proprioceptive drive and microscale theta remains sensitive to subsecond limb movements.

Neocortical circuits use synaptic and intrinsic forms of homeostatic plasticity to stabilize key features of network activity, but whether these different homeostatic mechanisms act redundantly, or can be independently recruited to stabilize different network features, is unknown. Here we used pharmacological and genetic perturbations both in vitro and in vivo to determine whether synaptic scaling and intrinsic homeostatic plasticity (IHP) are arranged and recruited in a hierarchical or modular manner within L2/3 pyramidal neurons in rodent V1. Surprisingly, although the expression of synaptic scaling and IHP was dependent on overlapping signaling pathways, they could be independently recruited by manipulating spiking activity or NMDAR signaling, respectively. Further, we found that changes in visual experience that affect NMDAR activation but not mean firing selectively trigger IHP, without recruiting synaptic scaling. These findings support a modular model in which synaptic and intrinsic homeostatic plasticity respond to and stabilize distinct aspects of network activity.

A number of cognitive and sensory processes are characterized by strong relationships between the timing of neuronal spiking activity and the phase of ongoing local field potential oscillations. The coupling of neuronal spiking activity in neocortex to the phase of alpha oscillations (8-12 Hz) has been well studied in monkeys but remains largely unexplored in other mammals. How these relationships differ between brain areas and cell types, and how they relate to somatosensory signal detection and decision making, are not well understood. We used high density microelectrode arrays to chronically record neural activity from somatosensory cortex, prefrontal cortex, striatum, and amygdala in mice performing a head-fixed whisker-based selective detection task. We observed strong spontaneous alpha phase modulation of single neuron spiking activity as mice performed the task. The prevalence and strength of alpha phase modulation differed significantly across regions and between cell types. Phase-modulated neurons exhibited greater changes in spiking activity during task execution than their unmodulated counterparts. Furthermore, alpha modulation of neuronal spiking during baseline activity correlated with task performance. In particular, many neurons selectively exhibited strong alpha modulation of spiking activity prior to correct trials, but not prior to incorrect trials. These data suggest that dysregulation of spiking activity with respect to the ongoing alpha oscillation may characterize lapses in task engagement or attention.

sample_q_texts: Over the past two decades, deep learning has progressed to become one of the most prominent statistical machine learning frameworks. Nonetheless, how deep learning achieves its impressive performance, both on supervised data and in out-of-distribution predictions, remains far from being fully understood. From a deep learning perspective, unsupervised pretraining achieves state-of-the-art results on a large variety of challenges (e.g., commonsense reasoning), and these models achieve impressive performance in out-of-distribution scenarios. This work explores the role of latent space in unsupervised pretraining using a coherent multi-layer LSTM baseline. We showed that unsupervised pretraining via latent space harnesses features that are already present in the input and thus maintain its effectiveness. This work generates a deep learning architecture that shows consistency in both supervised and out-of-distribution performance.

Text generation models have achieved impressive results on standard question and answer domains, but remain too expensive to train from scratch for a large variety of domains. Pretraining with extensive synthetic tasks requires a rare representation, called a Prompt Generation Memory (PGM) space, but these algorithms rely on a few Prompts to achieve high scores in tests with only a few Prompts. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of creating similar PGMs through a lower-cost and environment-friendly approach based on known log-linear inference. We introduce a training procedure to progressively learn embeddings of large ontologies, preserving the long-range dependencies that make log-linear inference perform better at inference speed. This enables the use of only two Prompts in standard evaluations, while many Prompts remain needed in real applications. Using knowledge distillation with Transfer Transformer (T5), we demonstrate that the applied procedure enables us to learn embeddings of multiple ontologies, and generate longer forms, in a scalable manner. This scalable approach provides a clear path to train large-scale models for questions and answer domains, avoiding common challenges for PGMs like computation latency and human supervision.

Well-trained deep neural networks (DNNs) like GPT-3, outperform traditional supervised learning with trained datasets in fine-grained language understanding. However, achieving this entails in-depth training, representing a significant computational investment compared to traditional unsupervised learning. Here, we introduce W3F, a practical and efficient foundation for achieving state-of-the-art in supervised domains. W3F employs novel model architectures and algorithm designs, and rigorously evaluates on real-world datasets. Experiments show W3Fs ability to obtain top-performing results with a minimal fraction of human intervention across three domains: Medical Diagnosis, Event Extraction, and the Census Narratives Task. In essence, W3F allows us to overcome the cost and time challenges of supervised learning and brings cutting-edge deep learning into everyday computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

Deep-learning models are often used to analyze, augment and generate annotated text data. However, when applied directly to a non-English text corpus, the models might generate erroneous translation hypotheses. In order to evaluate the performance of machine translation models on various text corpora, we compare three specific tasks, (i) translation on reference-written text (LSText), (ii) translation on text generated from an unsupervised domain adaptation model (RELABEL in the paper) (DA-RELABEL), and (iii) translation on text generated from an image dataset (ILSVRC 2017). We observe that most of the semantic concepts are correctly detected in these tasks, but translation to colloquial speech from text with accurate translation hypotheses makes language-specific difficulties. We consider that this indicates that models trained for LSText tasks may apply for interpretation or dubbing to diverse languages, but should only be used in domains where fine-tuned monolingual training corpora are available, e.g. to dialects of British or American English. This study provides important implications for how translation models can be improved for diverse contexts in languages where limited available corpora exists.

Spam, or bulk, spam is a common email spoofing target, where callers play a call center recording and pretend to be the same company the caller is dealing with. But it still poses a security issue, since these spoofing recordings can be very convincing, impersonating the real ones. A major challenge for security systems is to learn the true identity of the calling party in these recordings, through a supervised learning approach. Other methods of spoof detection are based on statistical analysis of telephony, but they are not robust in the presence of noise.

To address these problems, we propose a method that requires only unary timestamps to identify call origin. Given multiple voice calls from the same location and at the same time, the point of time at which each call ended at a T-cell in the sampled calls is extracted. Each T-cell is used to identify the caller. By this method, there is no need for a call center recording as a test database, and we developed a formalism that demonstrates the robustness of the method to various call environments.

Our method uses natural language processing to extract an identity vector that captures variation in sequence length, density and stop-start timestamps. It also uses a classifier that distinguishes genuine or copy from fake calls. The classifier includes a binary SVM classifier, as well as two Neural Networks: one for detecting deceptive timestamps and one for detecting mundane calls, to improve robustness. We further apply a POS-model to improve call center-related data.

Finally, we integrate this framework with two state-of-the-art bulk spam detectors: unBLUE (Anonymous caller informative Language-based detection using predictive text) and the Adaptive Phone Number System (AuNS) [Yu.M.Datta, SA.Sasidharan, S.Lee, Proc. - 17th International Conference on Automatic Speech Recognition. Hyderabad, India, pp.142-149, 2009].

Together with AuNS, our method achieves an accuracy of 97.4% in the detection of spam in a call center. In terms of standard deviations, it has the smallest standard deviations of any other method that has been evaluated against the AuNS, averaging ~600 offset phone number pairs detected per spam e-mail.
