Language processing is one of the highest priorities for computational science as it is the primary interface between the human and digital world. One promising approach to this challenge is to assemble the millions of human-readable human-reader interfaces in this digital world into computable representations. The common approach has been a dependency graph constructed from manual annotation. Here, we present Mindric, the first entity-aware, recursive dependency graph inferred from broad, unannotated text and multimodal data. Since our early version, we have automated the annotation of the graph by refining features automatically identified as dependencies, and we have experimentally demonstrated that our inference will work even when written, parsed, or transcribed text is not available. This prediction makes it much more reliable, broadly applicable, and applicable to a wide range of languages. We demonstrate full grammar extraction and ground truth human coreference and referential events in single-label human-readable text (i.e., portions of written and spoken language). This allows us to verify the ability of Mindric to infer grammar and coreference relations to the vast majority of the manually annotated text used to create the dependency graph. This will enable the application of Mindric to the synthesis of future humans-ready synthetic languages.

This work aims to provide a thorough assessment of the gendered treatment of language data and how this impacts the diversity of representations for gender. Based on the findings from previous work we developed new metrics for assessing data quality, quantity, and diversity and presented new algorithmic toolkits for computing these measures.

Methods: In this work we collected 7744 audio language corpora from four big platforms, including SQUASHy, Adeptus, Ivory and Vilsas. We automatically coded 104 domain roles for both male and female language in eight question-answer corpora for four platforms. Then we compared gender representation by analyzing the diversity for each corpora in the corpus, and the production diversity in the transcripts based on the length. Then we extracted audio from 10 participants who acted in each domain roles; and performed a named entity relationship extraction of the named entities and a semantic role labelling in the individual transcripts for each domain role, and compared these representation for gender gender representation across the corpora and performances on the named entities and the role labels.

Results: We found that on average 22.5% of the individual audio recordings in the corpora have different genders than their spoken gender. But in only 11.6% of the recordings these genders are written correct. The gender diversity (10.7%) for speech domains is significant higher than (8.2) for writing domains. The performance on named entities task of domain roles are slightly higher in spoken than writing domains. All recordings do not reveal the difference in gender representation across the corpora.

Conclusions: Our work provides the tools and methodology to assess and quantify the gender representation of big datasets, and to identify differences for transcripts

Open source natural language modeling approaches offer a proven answer to the urgent problem of cyberthreat data science. Yet, even when applied with an effective model the cyberattack outcome of open source training data is poorly predicted. This is caused by one key blind spot: why the resulting attack behavior is similar to that found in models trained on detailed threat indicators. We argue that training data sampled and released for an emergent threat that is not yet considered in the developed model is very likely to miss all the clues that would allow the model to predict the behavior of the attack. To mitigate this issue, we develop the attack-ready diffusion model incorporating a principle of expectation. Our results show that, compared to the actions of open source training data sampled from a comprehensive taxonomy of threat indicators, attack-ready diffusion correctly predicts many time-stamped cyberattack behaviors that are not in the taxonomy, e.g. typos, noises, and duplicity. Our statistical analysis illustrates why the attack-ready model leverages known elements in the attack lifecycle that the general practitioner does not know. The resulting utility of attack-ready diffusion for cyberattack exploration is demonstrated using case studies on international ransomware as a service (RaaS) campaigns. Our results have implications for future models of cyberattack.

A fine-grained framework for identifying and prioritizing empirical modeling needs is vital for increasing the productivity of empirical natural-language processing research. However, building a network of representative neural network models that can be used to classify instances from a given NLP task requires substantial resources. In this study, we evaluated and compared the performance of 13K NLP models in seven benchmark datasets for 19 independent tasks, including 15 for Named Entity Recognition (NER) tasks and four for Textual Similarity (TextSsim) tasks. We were able to improve the unsupervised extraction of features for NER tasks by training a single model, compared with other models with multi- or multi-head fusion of models. The framework is generalizable to a wide range of NER tasks, including recursive labeling (NER/RERE), Entity Extraction (NER/REE), entity annotation (NER/AA), Additive Tasks (NER/ATA), and Question Answering (NER/QAN). Overall, all the models were competitive or outperformed previous best models for these NER tasks, with a smaller proportion of variance explained by the models. We also collected and compared the tokenized output for these models based on a local pattern recognition approach and for combining these models with Senti-BERT. Our methodology will be helpful in enabling researchers to develop a uniform set of all researchers dedicated resources for training and testing models for a specific NLP task without manually selecting a single model for extracting features.

Phase-covariant natural language processing (NLP) approaches leveraging understanding relationships ("ROPs") typically assume canonical sequence-grounding assumptions, such as the reader-determined ground to attend to (G-G AT). The G-G AT assumption is an assumption that texts are both generated by the brain and read through its imagined ground in the reader-in-the-box model. Because these assumptions are typically ignored, they risk leading to model-misleading ROPs. To address this issue, we evaluate ROp-based tasks in three real-world domains: open-source medical NLP (S&M), social media discourse (S&M), and fictional fantasy (S&M). We test ROp models across a wide range of real-world tasks, on a wide range of corpora, and on a wide range of models. Our experimental data show that the predictions of ROp models in S&M, S&M, and S&M are comparable to the predictions of the relative models of SCIXX. We find that task selectivity and task complexity play a role in the ROPs. Interestingly, the relative models tend to perform better on more complex tasks than the taskspecific models. We also find that an ROp-based ROPs task has superior performance and predictability compared to the other three tasks.

Commonly-acquired artificial intelligence (AI) models trained on large datasets can propagate misinformation by selecting prominent examples and overestimating confidence. We address the apparent contradiction between these purported increases in uncertainty and a reduction in active knowledge between 2013 and 2021. This effect is further exacerbated by widespread use of Facebook, where this familiarity is even more pronounced and the presence of a large 'dropout' population raises the scale of significance. We propose a novel ground truth to monitor skepticism effects in AI models, incorporating a cross-validation approach, and define a new metric, the skepticism factor, to quantify the variance in confidence associated with each addition to dataset. Experiments with publicly available models demonstrate a clear reduction of this variance for an expanding public dataset in terms of mean and variance, driven by careful model design in "early adopters" and the distribution of confidence increases. Significant reductions in variance when selecting from a stratified population of users and the verification of a "society effect" are observed. These findings are relevant for detecting societal perceptions of AI in dynamic use cases and highlight their potential application across contexts, as well as their counterparts concerning the biases present in existing AI that are not accounted for in research.

Current human-computer interaction (HCI) research largely assumes a US-centric perspective, rooted in a US cultural and racial framework. However, some HCI textbooks explicitly reject European-American framing in favor of multiculturalism, with the aim of broadening perspectives and fostering inclusivity across various societies. This study aims to empirically assess whether and how textbook frameworks and their representation of human factors change across multicultural frameworks. Twenty-one undergraduate students participated in an HCI course where they wrote one to three case studies on home automation, covering the use of a computer. The human factors in these case studies were conceptualized using the conceptual model by the Zurich Group, featuring four dependent variables: interaction styles, affective states, time-related preferences, and emotional state. Qualitative analysis revealed that the diverse perspectives provided by the multicultural framework were more easily integrated into the existing conceptual model, often resulting in faster progress through the conceptualization process. At the same time, students often struggled to utilize certain concepts originating from a culturally specific perspective, highlighting the need for a more conscious incorporation of race and culture in future HCI textbook designs. Our findings underscore the importance of considering diverse frameworks in HCI textbook design for inclusive and equitable learning environments.

Multidisciplinary research typically relies on multivariate techniques to identify commonalities across a variety of sources of data. Existing approaches often suffer from overfitting with one approach potentially requiring the other two for a comprehensive model, including for missing data. This is a special case that might be difficult to solve, as suggested by recent Bayesian evidence, which is naturally missing data-robust. Here, we approach this problem by relying on unsupervised learning. In our absence-solution framework, each researcher is explicitly identified and held responsible for ensuring the correctness of this process. We validate our model by comparing approaches that ignore this problem (generating a “neutral” model), require all research participants to collaborate, and jointly learn for both data characteristics and task specifications. We quantify the potential losses to the completeness of the model and find that our solution maintains or improves aspects of the original missing data or co-task modeling problem. Overall, our findings suggest that an explicitly designed and trained adversarial mechanism can improve missing data and co-task models, capturing the positive attributes of both at once.

Adaptability is the key to success. Performance requirements change rapidly due to changes in technology, knowledge, infrastructure, personnel, market needs, and more. In this regard, organisations are faced with a growing pressure to adapt to a changing environment. To respond to such environmental change organisations develop a broad set of capabilities (or capabilities set) which defines how new systems can be operated, customised and developed. This notion is supported by Haboush at al. [Phys. B 2019, 146:351-354] in predicting capability evolution. In this study, we present a conceptual framework to better understand the underlying capability evolution mechanism as well as its impact on the current capabilities set of a firm. In particular, we perform an exploratory analysis of the impact of capability evolution on the current capabilities set of the South African Call Centre industry. This is conducted through the use of a scenario-based conjoint analysis. An analysis of selected capability sets (63 total) of Call Centre firms located in South Africa is performed. We observe that the evolution of capabilities of these firms lead to relocation and replacement of employees based on technological, knowledge and economic change. This change has a positive impact on the business, but also a negative impact on the business capabilities set, with the highest relocation and replacement costs for IT related capabilities, followed by capabilities pertaining to services and customer relations. Our results show that change has a strong impact on the capabilities set of a firm and also in the direction of the development of these capabilities.

Proving robustness of big data networks during scale-up and scale-down is important for successfully predicting unpredictable, critical outcomes of current and future machine learning models. A large-scale analysis of four-year workloads of a real-time sensing system capturing an explicit representation of phenomena, it has been previously shown that the system can be expected to lose or gain signals based on changes to design details, bandwidth and network configuration. In digital health, generating and understanding digital health data is paramount to driving medical advances in conjunction with statistics and data science. Despite their pervasive presence, many individuals remain unaware of the magnitude and potential applications of these information and analytics. This lack of awareness is especially relevant in the context of digital health, where patient data lies at the intersection of science and technology, influencing healthcare systems, practices, and patient outcomes. In this commentary, we explore the latest research conducted in digital health, which is intimately associated with privacy and security. We outline some of the common interpretations of these concepts, and how the intersection of privacy and security informs researchers and policymakers. We argue that this intersection presents an opportunity to further advance the field by leveraging privacy and security challenges to foster innovative digital health applications, while managing potential issues that may impede such progress. We highlight several specific issues in digital health that hold out promise for both technological and societal breakthroughs: anomaly detection, feature engineering, and machine learning algorithms. The discussion is driven by a series of questions that can be used to encourage future experimentation in digital health.

While minimizing model complexity without losing prediction accuracy, model performance is only ensured if the model fitness function increases with sample size. Furthermore, we know that human learning performance decreases with increasing sample size in active learning methods. To make the decision between sample sizes more transparent, we evaluate the accuracy of predictive models and conduct statistical tests against the prediction accuracies of models with different sample sizes. We investigate the effect of mean and variability on prediction accuracy as well as the fluctuation pattern of individual measurements. Our evaluation shows that the prediction accuracy of low-complexity, but high-variance predictive models is markedly higher than that of high-complexity, but low-variance predictive models. These results may provide a useful reference for medical data analysis in the context of active learning.

Objective/HEDensity of Diversity Network (DODINet) designed three diabetes-specific health literacy and numeracy content pieces and organized three structured feedback cycles to evaluate their value and effectiveness in supporting content. Methods/HEDenvelight Reading, a free, open-source, book-editing platform, was used to create drafts for three short, catchy, and memorable written content pieces, medical literacy and literacy apps, and video. Each feedback round began with an overview of the feedback about the draft content. Feedback categories and questions were identified, and each round was designed to gauge users familiarity with the topic, overall engagement, readability, and clarity. The main outcomes from this research are: (1) content was created to be "openly readable," and that readability scores within feedback rounds varied significantly, (2) content received high overall engagement, and (3) the sample group welcomed the opportunity to provide feedback on content items before they were completed, making it possible for staff at every level to include the content pieces in their work. This research provides insight to inform the future design of digital content that is more universally understandable.

Ambient air pollution has highly adverse effects on public health and the environment, particularly in urban areas of the Global South. Systematic air quality monitoring (AQM) is a precondition for effective policies to mitigate this problem, and making AQM data publicly available also signals commitment to take action. Thus far, little is known about the global capacity for public AQM, and how it varies across geographic location, pollution exposure, and socio-economic characteristics. We thus constructed a novel, geocoded dataset on AQM behavior in more than ten thousand urban areas of low to middle-income countries. In almost 90% of these urban areas, we are unable to identify any monitoring activity, and the form and extent of AQM in the remaining 10% varies greatly. Income levels and characteristics of political institutions (democracy) turn out to be key drivers of variation in AQM activity, with urban areas in more democratic countries more likely to respond with more AQM to high air pollution levels. The evidence provided here can serve as a wake-up call for public authorities, international institutions, and civil society stakeholders to invest far more than hitherto the case into AQM, particularly in under-monitored, less affluent, and less democratic settings.

Comparing averages requires knowing sample variation, which can be shown visually using a bar graph with error bars or a box plot. Because error bars and box plots can show different measures, they must be labelled to be interpretable. Of graphs of averages shown at a scientific conference in 2020, 87.5% of graphs did not contain enough information on the slide to interpret them. The only graphs that were fully interpretable (12.5%) were bar graphs. By comparison, 92% of graphs of averages published in a journal in the same field contained enough information to interpret them. While conferences are not and should not be as stringent about data presentation as journals, that a statistical value as simple as an average are not clearly presented suggests graphs are created by rote.

sample_q_texts: Slippery jet (SJ) is an extremely rich observational record of the atmosphere and its mesoscale physics, including both streamwise and vertical flux gradients, and turbulent changes in momentum, energy, and outflow. It provides vital constraints on processes such as boundary layer height decay, deep turbulent entrainment, and the initiation of intense westerly jets. Yet to date the statistical properties of SJ volumes are only weakly constrained by extant observational data. Here we report the first analysis of the nature and temporal variability of a discrete volume of pressure-driven flow observed in a series of remote sensing tracks within the Boundary Layer Dynamics-II archive. It was found to have a non-zero volume near the top and bottom of the upper and lower layers of the boundary layer, and represented the accumulation of both turbulent kinetic energy and momentum into a spatially extended volume. The tendency towards increasing flow density at all height levels, and also at all times, was characteristic of SSJ trends and is indicative of the presence of a buoyancy source. These observed nonlinearities arise from the combination of sink-source processes of SJs: driving-air-masses into a region of high variance from a jet-exit altitude, and their subsequent growth and detachment from the flow field with lift off. We interpret the magnitude of the sink-source gradients at various altitudes as a feedback on scale height and flow pressure.

Chemical reactions can only occur when energy is added in form of exergonic reactions. However, life on Earth probably did not arise until there was a steady influx of chemical energy from the sun. How the planets of our Solar System, particularly those in the main asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, gained this energy remains a mystery. Here, we examine the temporal and spectral patterns of chemical activity throughout the nebula that surrounds the Sun. All of the planets in the asteroid belt are active both in the UV and X-ray bands, supporting the hypothesis that a steady input of solar chemical energy was available to more active planets, such as Jupiter and Saturn. In addition, the change in chemical activity in planetial bodies is strongly correlated with periods of low solar variability.

Magnetospheric jets, including dipolar jets, drive multipoint magnetospheric and planetary-scale auroral phenomena such as magnetic substorms. Long-standing gaps in our understanding of magnetospheric dynamo processes at current plasma sheet regimes call for new tools that capture active-region magnetic reconnection (e.g., plasmoids) and help interpret the dominant heating and driving mechanisms of substorms. We first co-observe two different types of active-region plasmoids (i.e., southern and Northern; L and G sheets) on the Earth dayside in conjunction with energetic particle, energetic particle induced current, and ground magnetometer measurements in DMSP-F17. Specifically, we measured subthermal electrons and energetic particles, as well as magnetospheric column electron densities that were dominated by plasmoids in both latitude bins and localized plasmoids in the Northern shield. Following an onset of auroral substorm over the dayside, G and L substorm plasmoids emerge on the dayside, boosting the intensity of auroral substorm glow in the limb shadow region where auroral substorms typically occur. High-spatial resolution magnetometry measurements during the auroral substorm onset measured the first dipolar jet layer in the upper part of the dayside ionosphere, coinciding with plasmoid generation. We further studied the magnetic reconnection process via multi-scale frame-localized tau-mu-diffusion (FLMDT) tomography, obtaining the reconnections for energetic particles and current-carrying currents. Our results offer key insights into the reconnection process associated with substorm plasmoids that can guide both the future application of Rosetta Code and future observational studies.

Dynamically-evolving simulators such as GENESIS are used to predict the explosive capture (e.g. interaction with a plasma-mobile environment) of far ultraviolet (FUV) photon--e.g. Ly$sup_{2}{E}' $ from neutral-ion atmospheres. These simulations are typically performed on a ~3-dimensional continuum grid at various time and length scales. Simulations involving the local (p>12km), global (12^6s), and high-dimensional ($25^{100}-{1000}-{1000}rd$) redshift ranges that are classically associated with stellar interiors (typ. core hydrogen) are computationally very expensive. The techniques developed herein aim to increase the efficiency of FUV simulation involving clouds, including those on the genus star, Alpha Cen G$23{H}, by simulating the interaction of far ultraviolet light with a radiative atmosphere made up of Compton-thick interstellar dust grains.

Methodology1.

A novel line-broadening algorithm based on a combination of double-Gaussian and Gaussian processes was used to model the response of the dust to a known (obtained from a world-class one-dimensional (1-D) simulation) ionizing photo-ionization (IPI) dose given by observations of hydrogen Balmer emission lines from Accreting Low Mass X-ray Binaries (AMXBB) in the UV. A 1-D (5x3 grid) computational grid of clouds was generated from the continuum (Planck grid) and ionized (HaloGen), stellar (Spectrum-C), and dust (CC-Ritter) models. Computer simulations of the interaction of the FUV photon, accompanied by its excitation by the IPI and/or atomic hydrogen background, into the atmosphere were performed on a 10{Gpu} cluster run using the CTX-B1/Will8 codes.

The equilibrium mass current is a complex physical phenomenon that drives the magnetic field in convection-powerful plasmas and is one of the biggest astrophysical challenges that challenges modern astrophysical observations. While the usual form of equilibrium fields, e.g. the Brinkman ion thermal instability (IT), can generate equilibrium fields that are close to the equilibrium conditions, the magnetic fields generated can have substantial deviations and the formation of different structures like loops and filaments. This disconnect between equilibrium fields and their magnetic fields on the plasma scale is believed to be due to the physics of the fields upstream of the thermal plasma. Here we show that such a decoupling of the equilibrium fields is possible when the plasma is not in equilibrium at the local ion temperature (e.g. in the middle of a filamentary outflow) and that it leads to an anomalously small mean electron temperature. The observed cooling from the middle of the filament is not related to the reduction of the electron temperature in the filament itself but rather due to the reduced turbulence below the collisionless break when the electron temperature is reduced to a level below the OMNITHERM stability limit. We analyze the set of equilibria with the self-consistent numerical model to demonstrate the physics. We also quantify the effect of this cooling process on the spatial segregation of particles in an inhomogeneous plasma.

This work is based on the World Atlas of Magnetic Fields (WAoMF) project initiated by the Plasma Applied Geophysics Facility (PAGU), based on the plasma thermodynamics library "MagnetoTherm", including expert and machine learning-generated models based on ion thermal equilibriums and magnetic currents. The work is also based on the Phys-LIB software.

Importance and Relevance: The decoupling between equilibrium and applied fields in the process of formation of magnetic structures is a known phenomenon in laboratory experiments but has not yet been reproduced in the context of astrophysical diagnostics in a MHD-engine coupled code. This work thus opens up new possibilities for MHD physics.

Protoplanets are large planets within the protoplanetary disk that eventually result from the collision of planetesimals. However, protoplanets can be dynamically unstable, with rapid accretion, and loose structures can facilitate explosive formation. If protoplanets are unstable due to slow compositionally labile silicate protoliths at early stages in the planets evolution, then internal mechanisms, such as shock-enhanced melting or metasomatic enrichment, must be in play. Here we present analytical framework predictions that consider the combined consequences of nonspherically thin protolith compositions for the impact of protoplanet growth on the radial radial flux of emission-line molecules, using first-principles quasi-first-principles methods, as well as the expected conditions of a protostellar environment. We consider if destabilization of the protoplanet onto a planetesimal requires initial exposure to viscosity ratios exceeding three orders of magnitude. We further demonstrate the ability of our method to forecast protoplanet stability and nucleating gas accretion, and related growth, mass loss, or central cooling time constraints on the planets formation in young disks.

Gravity and gravity waves are two fundamental physical phenomena that shape the solar system. They are expected to affect every system that is dependent on gravity, including the Moon, the Sun, exoplanets, planetary satellites, and even the magnetic field of the Earth. It is important to better understand this phenomenon so that it can be observed and analyzed in a detailed and precise way, and also to obtain a better understanding of the effects of gravity and gravity waves on systems of different scales. Therefore, the present work involves the analysis of numerical model results and identification of complex dynamics in which the most common are damped gravity and self-gravity, by using the GENESIS software. Through this identification, we find that the force and energy production rates of these models exhibit a maximum at a given value of the mass of the planet, which supports previous theoretical and experimental work. However, the work investigates how these effects of gravity and gravity waves affect the structure and dynamics of the Solar System. We found that gravitational forces are crucial in the changes in the kinetic energy and other characteristics of the satellites, and that these effects are dependent on the mass of the satellite and its orbital distance, which strengthens the idea of the importance of this factor in the solar system.

Most white dwarf (WD) star simulations produce systems consisting of isolated white dwarf stars without either an external or internal angular momentum. As a WD star drifts through its evolution towards stellar death, it will gradually interact with its circumstellar medium and accelerate its internal angular momentum. Dispersed gravitational waves from this interaction can tear apart the equilibrium of outer planets of the WD star or disrupt the white dwarf star itself. These disruptions could influence the future evolution of neutron stars and black hole binaries. I present Nuc-Gene, an open-source software library for simulating gravitational waves that couples to the 2019 code NucEncode. In this paper, I describe how Nuc-Gene is used in the creation of fully hydrogen and helium runaway simulations of WD stars in order to study the effects of gravitational waves on their interactions with the outer planets and their evolution towards and subsequent encounters with neutron stars and black hole binaries. I then describe how the interactions with these objects depend on the properties of the outer planets and particularly the presence of a core holding debris from a previous planetary encounter. When a WD star encounters a neutron star or a black hole with a relatively thick planetary debris disk, the gravitational wave interactions can cause a severe disruption of the outer planets and the WD star itself. I also describe how this process can be used to study WD star cores that have originally consisted of two outer planets which were severely disrupted, or crossed by the nucleus of an earlier compact binary system, with each binary system resulting in a nuclear explosion of the remaining compact system.

HII galaxies in the context of dark energy simulations offer a unique opportunity for studying the evolution of the interstellar medium (ISM). We employ a novel method, combining three integral field spectroscopic surveys with a hydrodynamical N-body model and the LAMBDA-gas parameterization, to investigate the ISM evolution in the low-mass dark matter universe. We identify five HII galaxies and two low-mass infrared dark matter galaxies and characterize their chemistry. The obtained distribution function of HC2 (302.6 + 41.6/103.7 km/s), from which we obtained a 2.9 km/s smoothing length, exhibits many properties of molecular clouds with a star-forming history ranging from less than an hour to several million years, depending on the model parameters. The average collisional excitation level of the gas is E = 136 eV and the average gas column density increases significantly due to the successful chemical pumping by UV light. The gas density increases over the timescale of a few Myr from about 1 to several cm-3 and, even to extremely high column densities, the interplanar distribution is optically thin. In the simulations, the sub-mm continuum rises to a peak at a redshift z m > 2 with a luminosity of L mm > 10^(13)ergs/s. To reach these magnitudes, a fraction of the available millimeter radiation has to be reflected into the optical wavelength range, which our simulations suggest can occur within the host galaxy, even if the star formation rate is faster than the Cosmic Noon (cNO), indicating a more efficient star formation process in the simulations. However, we conclude that even for young galaxies such as the ones we model, star formation is not driven by the absence of photo-dissociation regions.

Satellite-based meteoroid detection techniques are now well established, and in recent years, a wide array of detectors has been developed to suit diverse needs. However, current synthetic meteoroid detection techniques are primarily focused on detecting larger, metallic objects, resulting in low coverage of smaller, less likely impactors. In this study, we introduce a research tool capable of processing up to thousands of METS-recognized data packets and identifying a specific information class, offering several benefits. Initially, the D3 dataset focuses on the detection of low-amplitude impact events with impact parameters less than 600 m. In order to monitor different environments and weather conditions throughout the day, the D3 dataset comprises 16 routes between MeteoNet observatories across Italy. Data from these routes are processed by our tool to classify data packets based on their geometric and kinematical parameters, providing a comprehensive picture of meteoroid trajectories and their potential impact on the environment.

This approach provides a new resource to understand diseases. TST is being extensively used to address the impact of cellular defects in tissue function and disease states in biomedicine and to develop new treatment approaches. By comparing spatial transcriptomic profiles across multiple tissues, transcriptomic spatial gene expression relationships can be uncovered. Systems biology aims to understand the components, proteins, pathways and interactions in diverse biological processes. An attractive means to achieve this goal is to use comprehensive omic data containing expression, physical and morphological measurements of biological objects such as cells, tissues, and organisms. While cell-level expression networks have been used to analyse dynamic changes of gene expression in time, characterizing the influence of physical features of the same type of objects have proven difficult due to limited availability of physical measurements across an organism and the lack of standard framework to automatically classify and integrate them in a common way. Here we present quantitative maps based on cell-level expression data generated using RNA-seq and proteomics using neurite tracing analysis and morphometric measurements of neurons and oligodendrocytes, respectively. In addition to objective evaluation of physical features of cells, we can choose samples with similar morphological and physiological characteristics within a given cell type, making it much easier to explore cell-specific differences in tissue organization. We provide a framework for integrating novel types of cell-level measurements into classical systems biology studies, including -fold expansion, translatability of extracellular networks and standardized metric quantification across measurements. We show quantitative maps for metrics used in physiology and cancer research, in addition to our novel cell-level quantitative maps for brain morphology.

BACKGROUNDOne of the biggest challenges in contemporary biology is uncovering cellular processes based on gene expression data. Spatial proximity analysis can help to address this need by leveraging genetic, physical and environmental information to capture cell states. Therefore, combining approaches from transcriptomics and spatial biology in a tight integration could strengthen the emergence of these new areas of biology.

METHODSWe performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of spatial proximity analyses using microarray data, supplemented with transcriptomics, environmental information, and connected gene expression. We report 37 studies from three types of spatial proximity analyses: Quantitative Spatial Modeling, Spatial Analyses on Spatial Scales, and Spatial Regression. We assessed how three dimensionality in time-space relationships in our sampled cells was transformed into spatial proximity scores. We demonstrated how spatial proximity scores can relate to cellular organisation and gene expression in three dimensions and compared its main results across different scales: (i) a typical cell contributes to multiple spatial proximity measures (ii) spatial proximity is more robust to deleting adjacent cells and (iii) cell size could have a determinant role in cellular organisation. We compared spatial proximity plots of shared expression change to similar adjacency plots of shared patterns in neighbouring cells. We analysed the relationship between cellular dynamics, spatial proximity and the spatial distribution of transcription.

RESULTSThree-dimensional spatial proximity plots showed that regulatory interactions tend to be connected in spatial proximity plots but not in adjacency plots. We observed similar properties in cells that were contaminated by endomembranes. Spatial proximity plots showed similar results regardless of the scale of the observation. However, several dimensions may be hidden in the cell state depending on which cell is being analysed. In other words, while there may be a linear one-dimensional relationship between proximity and chemical state, this relationship might not exist in spatial proximity. There is an age-related shift in dimensions with age, giving additional insight into cellular patterns with age. We found that cells of certain expression scores and cell-sizes in one part of the body are more strongly connected to neighbouring cells in the other part of the body than the same cells in the other part of the body. This is most likely due to the difference in the ability of the cells to exchange regulators. Very small cells are more connected to neighbouring cells because they have more direct contact and can use this ability to exchange. Large cells have a strong interaction with neighbouring cells because they do not have a good substitute in their area of influence. This may be driven by an absence of sufficient contact.

sample_p_texts: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has shown remarkable promise in pathology applications, shedding light on the spatial organization of gene expression and its relationship to the tumor microenvironment. However, its clinical adoption remains constrained due to the limited scalability of current sequencing technologies. While recent methods attempt to infer ST from whole slide images (WSIs) using pretrained image encoders, they remain restricted by limited gene coverage, organ-specific training, and the need for dataset-specific fine-tuning. In light of this, we introduce STPath, a generative foundation model pretrained on a large-scale collection of WSIs paired with ST profiles. This extensive pretraining enables STPath to directly predict gene expression across 38,984 genes and 17 organs without requiring downstream fine-tuning. STPath integrates multiple data modalities, including histological images, gene expressions, organ type, and sequencing technology information, within a novel geometry-aware Transformer architecture. Unlike previous methods that directly map WSIs to gene expression, STPath is trained using a masked gene expression prediction objective guided by tailored noise schedules, effectively balancing between capturing gene-gene dependencies and performing high-quality predictions. We evaluate STPath across 6 tasks spanning 23 datasets and 14 biomarkers, including gene expression prediction, spot imputation, spatial clustering, biomarker prediction, gene mutation prediction, and survival prediction. These results demonstrate STPaths strong ability to infer spatially resolved gene expression and reveal crucial pathological structures within tissue samples, underscoring its promise for scalable ST-based pathology applications.

State-of-the-art spatial proteomic and transcriptomic technologies can deeply pheno-type cells in their native tissue environment, providing a high throughput means to effectively quantify spatial relationships between diverse cell populations. However, the experimental design choice of which regions of a tissue will be imaged can greatly impact the interpretation of spatial quantifications. That is, spatial relationships identified in one region of interest may not be interpreted consistently across other regions. To address this challenge, we introduce Kontextual, a method which considers alternative frames of reference for contextualising spatial relationships. These contexts may represent landmarks, spatial domains, or groups of functionally similar cells which are consistent across regions. By modelling spatial relationships between cells relative to these contexts, Kontextual produces robust spatial quantifications that are not confounded by the region selected. We demonstrate in spatial proteomics and spatial transcriptomics datasets that modelling spatial relationships this way is biologically meaningful. We also demonstrate how this approach can be used in a classification setting to improve prediction of patient prognosis.

Advances in spatial profiling have resulted in the generation of multi-omic atlases that span biological scales. In general, multiple workflows are required for image registration, coordinate registration, and spot deconvolution to integrate modalities. To improve the throughput of registration of multi-omic cohorts, we introduce PIVOT, a user-friendly and open-source interface for streamlined nonlinear registration. We demonstrate PIVOTs strengths through registration of three multi-omic datasets, and show comparison of its performance to existing workflows.

The generation of spatial data in biology has been transformed by multiplex imaging and spatial-omics technologies, such as single cell spatial transcriptomics. These approaches permit a detailed mapping of cell populations and phenotypes within the tissue context, which reveals that tissues are complex ecosystems that include multiple organisational structures over different length scales. Quantitative methods for maximising the information that can be retrieved from these images have not kept pace with technological advances in platforms, and no standard methodology has emerged for spatial data analysis. Proposed pipelines are often tailored to individual studies, leading to a fragmented landscape of available methods, and no clear guidance about which statistical tools are best suited to a particular research question.

In response to these challenges, we present MuSpAn, a Multiscale Spatial Analysis package designed to provide straightforward access to well-established and cutting-edge mathematical tools for analysing spatial data. MuSpAn provides easy to use, flexible, and interactive access to quantitative methods developed from mathematical fields that include spatial statistics, topological data analysis, network theory, geometry, probability and ecology. Users can construct custom pipelines from tools across these fields to address specific biological problems, or conduct unbiased exploration of data for discovery spatial biology. In summary, MuSpAn is an extensive platform which enables multiscale analysis of spatial data, ranging from the subcellular to the tissue-scale.

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have revolutionized tissue architecture studies by capturing gene expression with spatial context. However, high-dimensional ST data often have limited spatial resolution and exhibit considerable noise and sparsity, posing significant challenges in deciphering subtle spatial structures and underlying biological activities. Here, we introduce SpaHDmap, an interpretable dimension reduction framework that enhances spatial resolution by integrating ST gene expression with high-resolution histology images. SpaHDmap incorporates non-negative matrix factorization into a multimodal fusion encoder-decoder architecture, enabling the identification of interpretable, high-resolution embeddings. Furthermore, SpaHDmap can simultaneously analyze multiple samples and is compatible with various types of histology images. Extensive evaluations on synthetic and real ST datasets from various technologies and tissue types demonstrate that SpaHDmap can effectively produce highly interpretable, high-resolution embeddings, and detects refined spatial structures. SpaHDmap represents a powerful approach for integrating ST data and histology images, offering deeper insights into complex tissue structures and functions.

Spatially resolved omics (SRO) technologies enable the identification of cell types while preserving their organization within tissues. Application of such technologies offers the opportunity to delineate cell-type spatial relationships, particularly across different length scales, and enhance our understanding of tissue organization and function. To quantify such multi-scale cell-type spatial relationships, we developed CRAWDAD, Cell-type Relationship Analysis Workflow Done Across Distances, as an open-source R package with source code and additional documentation at https://jef.works/CRAWDAD/.

To demonstrate the utility of such multi-scale characterization, recapitulate expected cell-type spatial relationships, and evaluate against other cell-type spatial analyses, we applied CRAWDAD to various simulated and real SRO datasets of diverse tissues assayed by diverse SRO technologies. We further demonstrate how such multi-scale characterization enabled by CRAWDAD can be used to compare cell-type spatial relationships across multiple samples. Finally, we applied CRAWDAD to SRO datasets of the human spleen to identify consistent as well as patient and sample-specific cell-type spatial relationships. In general, we anticipate such multi-scale analysis of SRO data enabled by CRAWDAD will provide useful quantitative metrics to facilitate the identification, characterization, and comparison of cell-type spatial relationships across axes of interest.

An important task in the analysis of spatially resolved transcriptomics data is to identify spatially variable genes (SVGs), or genes that vary in a 2D space. Current approaches rank SVGs based on either p-values or an effect size, such as the proportion of spatial variance. However, previous work in the analysis of RNA-sequencing identified a technical bias, referred to as the "mean-variance relationship", where highly expressed genes are more likely to have a higher variance. Here, we demonstrate the mean-variance relationship in spatial transcriptomics data. Furthermore, we propose spoon, a statistical framework using Empirical Bayes techniques to remove this bias, leading to more accurate prioritization of SVGs. We demonstrate the performance of spoon in both simulated and real spatial transcriptomics data. A software implementation of our method is available at https://bioconductor.org/packages/spoon.

Spatial transcriptomics is advancing molecular biology by providing high-resolution insights into gene expression within the spatial context of tissues. This context is essential for identifying spatial domains, enabling the understanding of micro-environment organizations and their implications for tissue function and disease progression. To improve current model limitations on multiple slides, we have designed Novae (https://github.com/MICS-Lab/novae), a graph-based foundation model that extracts representations of cells within their spatial contexts. Our model was trained on a large dataset of nearly 30 million cells across 18 tissues, allowing Novae to perform zero-shot domain inference across multiple gene panels, tissues, and technologies. Unlike other models, it also natively corrects batch effects and constructs a nested hierarchy of spatial domains. Furthermore, Novae supports various downstream tasks, including spatially variable gene or pathway analysis and spatial domain trajectory analysis. Overall, Novae provides a robust and versatile tool for advancing spatial transcriptomics and its applications in biomedical research.

Spatially resolved omics enable the discovery of tissue organization of biological or clinical importance. Despite the existence of several methods, performing a rational analysis including multiple algorithms while integrating different conditions such as clinical data is still not trivial. To make such investigations more accessible, we developed mosna, a Python package to analyze spatial omics data with respect to clinical or biological data and to gain insight on cell interaction patterns or tissue architecture of biological relevance. mosna is compatible with all spatial omics methods, it leverages tysserand to build accurate spatial networks, and is compatible with Squidpy. It proposes an analysis pipeline, in which increasingly complex features computed at each step can be explored in integration with clinical data, either with easy-to-use descriptive statistics and data visualization, or by seamlessly training machine learning models and identifying variables with the most predictive power.

mosna can take as input any dataset produced by spatial omics methods, including sub-cellular resolved transcriptomics (MERFISH, seqFISH) and proteomics (CODEX, MIBI-TOF, low-plex immuno-fluorescence), as well as spot-based spatial transcriptomics (10x Visium). Integration with experimental metadata or clinical data is adapted to binary conditions, such as biological treatments or response status of patients, and to survival data. We demonstrate the proposed analysis pipeline on two spatially resolved proteomic datasets containing either binary response to immunotherapy or survival data. mosna identifies features describing cellular composition and spatial distribution that can provide biological insight regarding factors that affect response to immunotherapies or survival.

Availability and implementationmosna is made publicly available to the community, together with relevant documentation and tutorials implemented as Jupyter notebooks to reproduce the result at https://github.com/AlexCoul/mosna

Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has transformed our understanding of tissue architecture and cellular interactions, but integrating ST data across platforms remains challenging due to differences in gene panels, data sparsity, and technical variability. Here, we introduce LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW, a novel framework for integrating imaging-based ST data from diverse platforms without requiring shared gene panels. LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW addresses ST integration through two key alignment tasks: feature alignment across technologies and batch alignment across datasets. Optimal transport-guided feature propagation adjusts data sparsity to match scRNA-seq references through graph-based imputation, enabling single-cell foundation models such as scGPT to generate unified features. Batch alignment then refines scGPT-transformed embeddings, mitigating batch effects while preserving biological variability. Evaluations on mouse brain samples from five different technologies demonstrate that LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW outperforms existing methods and is effective for cross-technology spatial gene program identification and tissue slice alignment. Applying LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW to five ovarian cancer datasets, we identify an integrated gene program indicative of tumor-infiltrating T cells across gene panels. Together, LO_SCPLOWLOKIC_SCPLOW provides a robust foundation for cross-platform ST studies, with the potential to scale to large atlas datasets, enabling deeper insights into cellular organization and tissue environments.

sample_q_texts: In our research, we analyzed the effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) on visual perception and the human visual system. The process of cortical modulation known as entrainment highlights how context-specific information is integrated into the perceptual processing. Entrainment is observed when the neural populations are organized into patterns that resemble the patterns observed in the environment. This coherence between the cortical patterns and environmental stimuli provides the neural basis for visual perception. This coherence can be demonstrated with the help of specific visual stimuli. TMS has proven to be a powerful tool for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this phenomenon. In the current review, we compare TMS-induced entrainment to standard variation, focusing on individual variations. We demonstrate how the alpha band, a low-amplitude oscillatory pattern identified in human visual evoked potentials, can be reliably entrained. TMS-induced entrainment also shows parallels to natural variation in alpha wave periodicity observed in sleep spindles, evoked brain activity in different time-windows, and frequency fluctuations in theta and alpha bands recorded from adult humans. The entrainment is generally robust to TMS protocols, demonstrating its inherent robustness to TMS design. This represents a significant advance in our understanding of the visual processing system.

Different assays have been developed for detecting non-discriminative, low-frequency (LF) epileptic discharges (LE) from different brain regions in order to evaluate the impact of anatomical constraints on the EEG LF threshold. This manuscript compares current methods by implementing a machine learning approach based on the most important features (MFIs) extracted from the LF biomarkers. We propose several variations of the algorithm which achieve significantly more accuracy than other methods. We consider the performance of our MFIs on three major paradigms. We compare with the model extracted by Kouger and Hunter which has the highest reported precision in the literature. We also investigate the impact of model complexity in the LF thresholds by reducing the MFIs to only 20 features in order to evaluate our approach as a baseline. We test our MFIs in 40 healthy subjects and 30 subjects affected with focal epilepsy. In healthy subjects we achieve significant improvements over the benchmark models while maintaining the performance on patients. We show that the LF biomarkers are still able to discriminate between LF memory and LF self-sustained activity (SLA). Overall, we provide an accurate model to better characterize LF biomarkers in the EEG LF threshold and demonstrate that MFIs can provide clinically-beneficial information.

Intensive investigations during brain function explore the mechanisms governing how a synaptic response is encoded in the brain. To test our hypothesis that small-scale recordings are necessary for capturing synapse behavior, we use an application from the conventional intracranial EEG (IEMG) settings, namely conductance or delay mode. Electrode types were bipolar and multi-polar, ranging from Capillas: Stanford Neurophotonics 200-series. Tying electrode configurations to a priori knowledge of recorded tissue microstructure, we show that the multimodal data that arises from recordings of small-scale conductance (sensing) is in full accordance with known micro-circuit tissue constituents, such as myelin, and has large statistical power. We additionally present recordings from a new device, termed Feasibility Electrode (FE), which shows an unusual robustness to noise.

Future applications include exploring micro-circuit EEG's utilization in unbiased investigation of synchronized or competing components within the same multi-cellular circuit. As EEG micro-stimulation is broadly compatible with active neurophysiology, it is a promising platform for studies of physiological brain activity.

Epilepsy is a chronic disorder with significant behavioral, emotional, and social effects. The hallmark symptoms of uncontrolled seizures, particularly, are cognitive impairments, which are attributed to the role of the brain hemispheres in interaction. Many cases involve cortical projection loops to the brain stem and midbrain, making seizures a direct consequence of brain-to-brain interactions. Research highlights the key importance of functional connectivity in understanding brain dynamics, both in sleep and wake, and the influence of brain rhythms in seizure generation. Recent studies have emphasized the significance of emotional circuits in epilepsy, revealing the impact of external stimuli on the brain under ictal and interictal conditions. Despite advancements in imaging techniques, mapping the circuit maps of epilepsy remains a significant challenge, especially in comparison to its counterpart in healthy people. This challenge involves discerning the connection between neuropsychiatric disorders and epilepsy, which distinguishes normal brain dynamics from epileptiform patterns. Ultimately, we aim to develop a method for the automatic prediction of ictal and interictal hemodynamic correlates for seizures.

Author SummaryThe standard map of brain dynamics lacks an explanatory framework based on local connectivity in subjects with seizure disorder. In our work, we identify functional connections between the cortex and other brain regions with significance for seizure generation. We propose a method for automatic prediction of ictal and interictal correlates for seizures. Our method reveals a link between seizure onset and anatomical connectivity between distinct brain regions. We validate our approach with healthy data, identifying specific functional connectivity patterns in epilepsy, including coronal projections that reflect ictal dynamics and coronal trajectories reflecting interictal processes. This work provides insights into seizure propagation and paves the way for practical applications in monitoring seizure activity to prevent further seizures.

Several epilepsy therapies target structural brain changes, but these therapies may also suppress seizures during onset, resulting in disease relapse. To improve this balance, we evaluated the effects of moderate combined psychopharmacological treatment (phonophoresis + lanoxin) with structural neuroimaging techniques (MAGNETO+TOMO) on induced seizures. Subjects were treated with 12 daily sessions of phonophoresis and lanoxin. The treatment protocol was applied to 18 healthy volunteers with control subjects and two weeks of sham treatment: one of them received lanoxin and phonophoresis. Structural imaging were performed during each session with focused magnetics 7.4T-MR and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) using a uniform axial diffusion sequence to measure a myelin-associated white matter population. During behavioral testing, we recorded electrical activity using two ambulatory video-EEG devices. Lanoxin doses decreased the premotor phase of the first baseline (between 50% and 100% decrease) and enhanced activity during the vagal response (period of the first phase following suppression) in sham and dose groups. Regarding drug-induced seizures, each group was exposed to a 6-day stimulation protocol simulating e.g. carrageenan-induced or ischemic seizures. During that phase, every pre-electrodesignal was analyzed with MRI-7.4T to monitor diffuse axonal injury and epileptogenic activity. As epileptogenesis progresses, the local field potential, the EEG, DTI, and structural MRI. These techniques suggested that low-doses of lanoxin can be beneficial when combined with phonophoresis in individuals at risk of seizures.

Author SummaryStructural MRI revealed a relative sparing of thalamic thalamocortical afferent fiber pathways following lanoxin, and the sham controlled paradigm did not show any seizures despite seizures in others. While the afferent system is poorly understood in epilepsy, we found early neuronal hyperexcitability in the precentral and supplemental motor area combined with alterations in the axonal myelination of the primary and secondary motor cortex. This corresponds to the slowing down of basic brain circuits from spontaneous waves to suppression of the GABAergic activity of the subnuclei of Putamen.

Biological oscillations are a defining feature of biology and involve persistent central and peripheral activity such as fluctuations in neural field potentials, pacemaker discharges, systemic and tissue perfusion rhythms, and muscle activity. Understanding the functional differences of these oscillations is key to understanding their role in both the functional connectivity of neural circuits and in the activation of cells within these circuits. Non-linear representations of the power spectrum provide a metric to characterize oscillations by averaging and expressing variations across fixed time-spans, enabling applications such as detecting oscillations within auditory cortex and characterising modulatory interactions across oscillatory frequencies. However, these calculations typically rely on temporal cross-correlations within recordings. In this study, we propose a method to perform non-linear averaging on frequency-independent power spectra, thereby circumventing the need for cross-correlation data. We demonstrate that such average power spectra are able to capture the structure of biological oscillations and estimate the occurrence of aberrant connectivity in entire functional networks, elucidating these oscillations from grey matter to white matter. Our method improves upon existing approaches, providing a reliable and detailed dataset enabling the study of oscillatory dynamics and the specification of neuronal functions and interactions beyond simple frequency-dependent averaging.

Nörocortical regions are rich in resting potential dynamics, but few studies have delineated which systems and processes drive these changes. By leveraging magnetoencephalography (MEG) neuroimaging from 76 healthy human subjects, we analyze the temporal dynamics of cortical activity across four seizure-frequency conditions in order to dissect resting-state properties that drive neuronal oscillations, including "rest landscape" (e.g., V and B-field populations, R1-frequency) as well as rhythm-independent activity (e.g., P300, Gpf, Delta). We show that these properties are invariant across seizure frequency and that the overall resting-state-to-seizure transition is well characterized by only two relevant amplitude-contributing system layers--the extra- and intracortical theta-1 frequency complex (thus "an undifferentiated" and "focal" aspects) and the inter- and intracortical theta-frequency neural population (thus "broad" and "Harriss-Heimann" aspects), with the latter being stronger during seizure. We further show that the average and spatio-temporal dynamics of these five activity networks converge to a "wide world state" at the rise of a seizure, with spiking activity oscillating at a ~70% rise rate and bursting amplitude (~3.3%) across the neuronal network. We support this interpretation with experiment, showing that ictal bursts in the frontal lobe of patients with epilepsy have reduced average "wide world" time and increased bursting amplitude (compared to control groups) even at seizure onset. These time-dependent oscillations further suggest a potential "rest rebound" or early seizure escape, such as during sleep. Importantly, we found that the particular network scaling of these properties (and seizure-period event durations) remained unchanged across seizure frequency conditions, offering a generalizable explanation for possible features of sustained regional electroencephalographic response. Our results show that spontaneous cortical oscillations drive and stabilize the waveforms of event-related neural activity across seizure frequency conditions and that both oscillations and activity-dependent processes are essential components of a rich temporal landscape in the somatosensory cortex.

Microscopic examination of the brain in epilepsy is consistently utilised to direct epilepsy surgery. However, not all of the brain structures studied are included, and for some these may not represent the entire seizure network, making them non-diagnostic, when epilepsy surgery is required. Current standardised epilepsy diagnosis requires intra-operative sampling of the hippocampus, but this is often only taken from the vicinity of the seizure, lacking sampling of key non-Seizure related structures. Furthermore, the quality of sampled tissue depends heavily on the expertise of the cutting personnel, and the vast majority of epilepsy surgical samples collected are single sections of tissue, resulting in limited sample size. This challenges consistency between samples, resulting in differences between studies. In particular, the difference in sample volumes between stereotaxic recordings and epilepsy surgery has limited the utility of stereotaxic seizure recordings when making decisions regarding the patient's likelihood of seizure in the future, or for individuals who have experienced seizures after surgery.

Here we develop a whole-brain epilepsy brain segmentation tool which allows recording of the entire brain and hippocampal network to be effectively studied when performing epilepsy surgery. We evaluated the accuracy of this tool in diagnosing seizure activity before and after treatment. Additionally, we quantified the presence of hippocampal active region segmentation in surgery teams to investigate the underlying issues that are limiting the representation of the hippocampal network in epilepsy surgery, particularly given that records often only include single tissue samples, with limited size. Ultimately, our final tool offers a tool for epileptologists, clinicians and students that enables the continued development of a routine for recording hippocampal activity during seizure surgery.

Highlights1. A whole-brain epilepsy framework which can effectively segment brain structures.2. The integration of hippocampal network segmentation with spatial and temporal epilepsy coding is shown to reduce variability in the recorded data and provide clinically accurate assessment for seizure detection.

Segmentation accuracy ranged from 74.2% to 98.8%. Using validated manual analysis criteria, the algorithm accurately discriminated between a confirmed positive and negative resection for 98.3% of the time and around 88.6% sensitivity (95% confidence interval 81.6-94.9), demonstrating that the tool can accurately detect epileptiform activity before and after surgery.
